catalogTitle: יו"ט של יובל; שיר השירים; והשתוקקות לגאולה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Pesach as the level of yovel and the fiftieth gate, above the seven of Shabbos, and from it explains why Hillel alone knew that the Pesach offering overrides Shabbos, why David found the place of the Mikdash, and why Shlomo and Moshiach carry the light of the final redemption.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Rashi's comment that the word 'im' by the omer and by yovel means an obligation, and with the Gemara's story of Hillel, who alone knew that the Pesach offering overrides Shabbos and was made Nasi. He sets beside it Doeg's envy of David for finding the place of the Mikdash. Using Sefer Yetzirah's three dimensions of world, year and soul, he explains that above the seven days of creation stands the level of 'pele', the fiftieth: yovel in time, the Mikdash in place, and the king in the soul. Pesach is the fiftieth gate, so it overrides Shabbos, which is only seven. David is Shabbos and Shlomo, his inner self, is yovel; Hillel is a gilgul of Shlomo, which is why he knew the halacha. The Mashgiach ends with Shir HaShirim's closing plea, the hard galus of Yishmael, and a call to daven on Pesach with emunah for the redemption.

en: Above the seven of Shabbos and shmitah stands the fiftieth, yovel, which is 'pele', beyond measure and understanding; Shavuos and Matan Torah, the Mikdash and Pesach all belong to it.
The place of the Mikdash is not named in the Torah because it is above 'place'; it must be sought, and only David, the 'reishis' and king of the soul, could find it.
Pesach is the fiftieth gate, which is why the Pesach offering overrides Shabbos, which is only the level of seven.
David is the seventh, Shabbos, while his inner depth, revealed in his son Shlomo who built the Mikdash, is yovel; Shlomo's era is a model of the days of Moshiach.
Hillel knew that Pesach overrides Shabbos because he is a gilgul of Shlomo, from the root of yovel, and not only because he had learned it from Shemaya and Avtalyon.
The Mashgiach says the days of Pesach are days of geulah and a time to daven, with emunah in Hashem alone, for the final redemption.

title.en: 'Im' by the omer and by yovel

summary.en: During the days of the omer the Mashgiach cites Rashi that 've'im takriv' by the omer means an obligation, proven from 've'im yihyeh hayovel', and asks why the Torah uses 'im' by yovel. He then begins the Gemara's account of an Erev Pesach that fell on Shabbos, when the Bnei Beseira did not know whether the Pesach offering overrides Shabbos.

title.en: Hillel becomes Nasi

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Hillel ruled that Pesach overrides Shabbos, how the Bnei Beseira stepped down and made him Nasi, how he rebuked them and then forgot the law of carrying the knife until he saw what the people did. He brings the Rema MiPano that the kingship of Torah stayed with Hillel's family because he descends from David.

title.en: Doeg's envy and the three dimensions

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Zevachim that David and Shmuel determined the place of the Mikdash, and that Doeg, a greater scholar, envied David for it, which he likens to the Bnei Beseira and Hillel. He then brings Sefer Yetzirah that the world exists in place, time and soul, each with its 'king' and beginning, called 'pele'.

title.en: Above the seven: yovel and the fiftieth day

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the seven days of creation and the middos from chesed to malchus have something above them: after shmitah comes yovel, after seven weeks of sefirah comes the fiftieth day, Shavuos and Matan Torah, 'bimshoch hayovel'. A slave whom the seventh year cannot free goes free at yovel, and Moshe added the fiftieth day because it is above reckoning.

title.en: The Mikdash, a place above place

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Beis HaMikdash is the place of yovel and 'pele': the Sanhedrin goes up there for a matter that is 'yipalei', and the Aron took up no space. Therefore the Torah gives no directions to the place of the Mikdash, only 'lishichno tidreshu', which he links by gematria to 'reishis'.

title.en: David, king of the soul, finds the Mikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the king is the 'pele' of the soul: even Shmuel did not know which son of Yishai was the king, just as the place of the Mikdash must be sought. Only David, the soul of Adam HaRishon and the 'reishis', could find the place, which answers Doeg's envy.

title.en: Pesach, the fiftieth gate

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Nissan is the head of time and Pesach comes from the fiftieth gate, which Jews receive as a gift on the Seder night and then work toward through sefirah. He brings the Maharal on why Haman fell on the first day of the omer, and explains that Pesach is yovel and therefore overrides Shabbos.

title.en: David is Shabbos, Shlomo is yovel

summary.en: The Mashgiach links Rosh Chodesh Nissan to the Kodesh HaKodashim and to 'kinas beischa'. He brings Rav Tzadok HaKohen that a father's inner self is revealed in his son: David is the seventh, Shabbos, and his inner depth, yovel, came out in Shlomo, who built the Mikdash and whose reign the Rambam's picture of Moshiach resembles.

title.en: Hillel, Shlomo, and the fiftieth Exodus

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam that Moshiach must come from Shlomo, and the Rema MiPano that Hillel is a gilgul of Shlomo. He asks why the Seder expounds 'Arami oved avi' and answers that the fiftieth mention of the Exodus, belonging to the days of Moshiach, is there; therefore Pesach overrides Shabbos, and the Bnei Beseira could not know it.

title.en: Hillel's ruling from the root of his soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Seder night is a time of asking without knowing, and that Hillel's ruling revealed the fiftieth gate because he is Shlomo, so the kingdom was set in his hand. Hillel credited Shemaya and Avtalyon out of humility, so Heaven made him forget the knife, revealing that his knowledge came from his soul's root. This also explains 'im' by the omer and yovel.

title.en: Shir HaShirim's last plea and Har HaMoriah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the days of Pesach are days of geulah, when a Jew must long for redemption. Shlomo ends Shir HaShirim with 'berach dodi', a plea that Hashem flee the galus with His people to Har HaMoriah. Yet today Yishmael holds that place, and he brings the Chasam Sofer that korbanos cannot be offered because Yishmael will not let a Jew go up.

title.en: The galus of Yishmael, 'pere adam'

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam's Igeres Teiman that no galus is harder than that of Yishmael, from 'oyah li' in Tehillim, and that Yishmael hates peace. He brings Rav Chaim Vital that 'bekum aleinu adam' refers to Yishmael, the 'pere adam', and the Chofetz Chaim's warning that a Yishmaeli remains a 'pere adam' whatever he becomes.

title.en: 'Adam velo melech'

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the same passuk refers to Haman, 'adam velo melech', and the Bnei Yissaschar that the seven nations parallel the seven middos and the Girgashi, as malchus, accepted Hashem's kingship and left. Achashverosh as a king had a spark of malchus, Haman did not; Yishmael too has only princes and no king, which makes his galus so hard.

title.en: Only Hashem can help: davening on Pesach

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yishmael is the impure side of yesod, a Friday that never reaches Shabbos, and that only Hashem can save from him, not politics or the military. Pesach, a time of revealed Shechinah, is the time to daven with emunah in Hashem and in tzaddikim for the redemption and for 'berach dodi'.

catalogTitle: א יום טוב פון אמונה דרשה לילדי תפארת יונה

oneLiner.en: Speaking to children, the Mashgiach explains that Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, the first believer, and that its matzah and its 'great wealth' are emunah in Hashem.

abstract.en: Addressing children, the Mashgiach opens by calling Pesach the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu: Avraham was the first Jew, Pesach is the first Yom Tov of the year, and Avraham is the one figure in the Torah of whom it is written that he ate matzos. He was also the first of whom the Torah says that he believed in Hashem. Since matzah is called the food of emunah, eating it with joy plants emunah in a Jew for the whole year. The Mashgiach describes that emunah: Hashem stands over a person and sees and knows everything he does, says and thinks, so how could he sin; Hashem can do everything, so one may rely on Him and not worry. He then shows how Avraham's own life ran on Pesach, and how the 'great wealth' promised to Avraham is, for every Jew, emunah. He closes with the coming Pesach of the future, when Moshiach will say he came because of the children who learned, davened and kept away from aveiros.

en: Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu: he was the first Jew, Pesach is the first Yom Tov, and he is the one tzaddik in the Torah of whom it says he ate matzos.
Matzah is the food of emunah; eating it with joy gives a Jew emunah for the whole year.
Emunah means believing that Hashem stands over a person and sees everything he does, says and thinks, which keeps him from sin.
Since Hashem can do everything, a Jew can rely on Him and need not worry about what he needs.
The 'great wealth' with which Jews leave Pesach is emunah, the greatest treasure a Jew owns.
In the future redemption Moshiach will say that he came because of the children who learned Torah, davened and kept away from aveiros.

title.en: Pesach, matzah and Avraham's emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the children that Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, the first Jew and the first in the Torah who believed in Hashem and ate matzos. Since matzah is the food of emunah, eating it with joy gives emunah for the whole year.

title.en: Hashem stands over us; the true great wealth

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that emunah means knowing Hashem sees everything and can do everything, so one keeps from sin and relies on Him. He shows how Avraham's life ran on Pesach and that the 'great wealth' promised to Avraham is, for every Jew, emunah.

title.en: The great Pesach of the future

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the future Pesach when Hashem will gather Jews from every land, ties it to the haftarah of the dry bones, and says Moshiach will credit the children who learned, davened and avoided aveiros. He closes by urging joy and emunah through the rest of Pesach.

catalogTitle: The Sweetness of תורה One Feels when Learning Properly

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yaakov did not need to teach Yosef Seder Taharos because Yosef's soul was rooted in taharah, and that only through kedushah and taharah does a person taste the true sweetness of Torah, tefillah and Shabbos.

abstract.en: Opening the weeks of Shovavim with the theme of taharah, the Mashgiach brings the Ba'al HaTurim that the word zekunim stands for five orders of the Mishnah, without Taharos, and asks why Taharos is missing and why Yaakov taught only Yosef. He also asks what Yaakov saw in the grain from Mitzrayim. He explains that the seven shepherds of Klal Yisrael, Yosef among them, stand above the tribes, and that the orders of the Mishnah correspond to them, with Taharos belonging to Yosef the tzaddik. Each tzaddik knows the Torah of his own middah by himself, as every creature knows by nature what it needs; so Yosef needed no teaching in Taharos. Because a tzaddik's possessions do not spoil, Yosef's grain kept the taste and smell that fruit lost when taharah ceased, and Yaakov sensed through it that Yosef was alive. The Mashgiach concludes that the taste of Torah and Shabbos comes only with kedushah and taharah, the work of Shovavim.

en: According to the Ba'al HaTurim, zekunim stands for the orders of Zeraim, Kodashim, Nashim, Yeshuos (Nezikin) and Moed, which Yaakov taught Yosef; Taharos is missing.
The seven shepherds (ro'im), the Ushpizin, are higher than the tribes because they lead all of Klal Yisrael, and Yosef is one of them.
Each of the six orders of the Mishnah corresponds to one of the Avos and tzaddikim, and Taharos corresponds to Yosef, the only one called 'the tzaddik', because he withstood his test.
Each tzaddik is rooted in one middah and knows by himself the part of the Torah tied to it, just as every creature knows by nature what it needs.
Whatever belongs to a tzaddik does not deteriorate, so Yosef's grain kept the true taste and smell, and through it Yaakov sensed that Yosef was in Mitzrayim.
The Mashgiach teaches that one can merit Torah, and feel the taste of Shabbos, only through kedushah and taharah, and that the weeks of Shovavim are the season to work on this.

title.en: Ben zekunim without Taharos

summary.en: Opening the weeks of Shovavim, the Mashgiach brings Rashi and the Ba'al HaTurim on 'ben zekunim' and asks why Taharos is missing and why Yaakov taught only Yosef. He then asks what Yaakov saw when he 'saw that there was grain in Mitzrayim', since everyone knew it.

title.en: The seven shepherds above the tribes

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the seven ro'im, the Ushpizin, lead all of Klal Yisrael while each tribe's head leads only his tribe, and that in the future the river will split into seven for them. Yosef was raised from a tribe to a ro'eh, as the pesukim and Rashi on 'even Yisrael' show.

title.en: The orders of the Mishnah and the Avos

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the Chok LeYisrael, which assigns each weekday an order of the Mishnah matching its middah, and shows which order belongs to Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov. Taharos belongs to Yosef, the only one called 'the tzaddik' because he withstood his test in Mitzrayim.

title.en: Why Yosef needed no teaching in Taharos

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Yaakov had to learn Torah from others while Avraham knew it by himself. He answers that each tzaddik is rooted in one of the seven middos and knows its Torah innately, like animals born knowing their craft; Avraham's chesed spans everything, while Yosef knew Taharos by himself, which answers the opening questions.

title.en: Shemiras habris, da'as and Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one who guards the bris like Yosef merits da'as, which is taharah, and Shabbos, since Yosef is Friday which prepares for Shabbos. He brings the Midrash that Shabbos is mentioned only by Yosef among the tribes, and that the nasi of Ephraim brought his offering on Shabbos.

title.en: The taste and smell of Yosef's grain

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that fruit lost its true taste and smell when taharah ceased, while a tzaddik's possessions do not deteriorate, so Yosef's grain did not spoil and kept its taste. Tasting that grain, Yaakov sensed a great tzaddik in Mitzrayim and hoped it was Yosef; the Mashgiach connects this to gematrios of 'yesh shever' and 'ben zekunim'.

title.en: Taharah brings the sweetness of Torah and Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ma'or VaShemesh that without taharah one cannot merit true Torah, and says the same holds for feeling the taste of Shabbos, which some find a burden. He mentions the Chazon Ish's instruction about boys' clothing for learning with clean hands, and ends that in Shovavim one must learn and daven with kedushah and taharah to feel their joy.

catalogTitle: בליל הסדר זוכים לגילוי שכינה כל אחד לפי מדריגתו

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Pesach, the yom tov of Avraham Avinu, is the foundation of all the moadim because it plants emunah, and that at the Seder each Jew, according to his level, receives emunah and a measure of gilui Shechinah, and through telling the makkos draws salvation for Klal Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the three regalim as the inheritance of the three Avos: Pesach is Avraham's yom tov of chesed and emunah. The Seder exists to plant emunah, and each person, by his level, receives some gilui Shechinah, as shown by a story of the Seer of Lublin. Mitzrayim was the kelipah of denial, so emunah, the root of all mitzvos, comes before Shavuos. Since the moadim are the lifeblood of Klal Yisrael, Pesach is the head of them all, and only Pesach-related mitzvos carry kareis. Matzah is the food of emunah that becomes part of one's flesh. A tzaddik is measured by his emunah. The makkos rose from water to the heavens to answer Pharaoh, and they mirror the ten utterances of creation in reverse. Telling them again brings them about again, so the Mashgiach urges saying the Haggadah with fire, closing with a simple Jew whose sincere bracha annulled a decree.

en: Pesach is the yom tov of emunah, inherited from Avraham Avinu, and the Seder is meant to plant emunah in every Jew.
At the Seder each Jew, according to his level, merits some revelation of the Shechinah.
Pesach is the head and foundation of the moadim; although Shavuos and Sukkos are higher, only the Pesach-related mitzvos carry kareis.
Matzah is the food of emunah: Hashem placed the emunah of that night into a food so that it becomes part of a Jew's flesh and blood.
Whatever happened at Yetzias Mitzrayim happens again each year, and telling the makkos at the Seder draws blows upon the enemies of Israel and healing for the Jews.

title.en: Pesach, emunah and gilui Shechinah at the Seder

summary.en: The Mashgiach links the three regalim to the three Avos, Pesach being Avraham's yom tov of chesed and emunah. The Seder is meant to plant emunah, and each person receives some gilui Shechinah by his level, as shown by the Seer of Lublin lifting his tallis at 'u-ve-mora gadol'.

title.en: Mitzrayim as denial; emunah before mitzvos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Mitzrayim was the kelipah of denial, as Pharaoh said 'I do not know Hashem', so leaving it means knowing Hashem. Through the dispute of the Ramban with the Rambam he shows that emunah is the foundation of the mitzvos, which is why Pesach precedes Shavuos and is called the head of all the moadim.

title.en: The moadim depend on Jews in Eretz Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that sanctifying the month can only happen in Eretz Yisrael, and that Hillel's fixed calendar works only because Jews living there, even simple farmers, keep it. He cites the Rambam that it is Hashem's kindness that Jews never ceased from the land, since without the moadim Klal Yisrael could not live.

title.en: Matzah, the food of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Pesach heads the moadim because Avraham, who gave his life for emunah, heads the Avos. The great clarity of emunah at makkas bechoros was placed by Hashem into the matzah so it would be absorbed into flesh and blood; every yom tov has such a food.

title.en: Why only Pesach carries kareis

summary.en: The Mashgiach ranks the regalim: Pesach is Avraham's level, Shavuos higher, Sukkos higher still. Yet only Pesach's mitzvos (chametz, the korban Pesach, and milah which holds it back) carry kareis, showing that Pesach, the foundation, binds a Jew to Hashem most deeply.

title.en: Telling the story; a Jew is measured by emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that through telling Yetzias Mitzrayim to the children emunah is absorbed. He cites the Chasam Sofer, who lengthened the telling and barely had time to eat before midnight, and discusses the deadline of chatzos. A tzaddik's tefillin are greater than a simple Jew's only through greater emunah.

title.en: The makkos as an answer to Pharaoh

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the makkos as Hashem's answer to Pharaoh's denial. The three groups each open with a passuk about knowing Hashem at a different level, and the makkos rise from water through earth, fire, air and the luminaries up to the souls of the firstborn, showing Hashem rules from bottom to top.

title.en: Makkos, the ten utterances, and retelling

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Yetzias Mitzrayim recurs every year. The ten makkos reveal the ten utterances of creation in reverse order, and lead to the Ten Commandments. Retelling makes it happen again, as with the son of Reb Yechezkel of Kuzmir, whose retelling of his father's miracle healed another sick man.

title.en: Saying the Haggadah with fire for salvation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Haggadah multiplies the makkos because saying them draws more blows on the enemies and more healing for Israel, according to one's fervor, and he urges saying it with fire in the danger now facing Eretz Yisrael. He explains spilling wine from the cup and closes with the Ropshitzer and Rimanover, who saw a simple Jew's sincere bracha annul a decree.

catalogTitle: צד א: הנחיצות שהמצות יאפו ע"י יר"ש

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the holiness of matzah, like that of a sefer Torah, comes from Hashem through a messenger acting lishmah, and so the matzos should be baked by G-d-fearing people with kavanah and joy.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Chesed L'Avraham: in the thirty days before Pesach, Hashem takes the Jews out of the klipah of Mitzrayim a thirtieth each day, and one must prepare for it through daily remembrance of yetzias Mitzrayim and accepting the yoke of Heaven. He brings the Ohr HaChaim that in Egypt the Jews sank to the forty-ninth gate of impurity, while before Moshiach they will reach the fiftieth, from which only the power of Torah can bring them out; this is how he reads the rasha of the Haggadah. He explains that Pesach, whose penalty is kares, is the foundation that binds a Jew to Hashem, the time of emunah, and matzah is its food. Then, from the sofer who is only Hashem's messenger, he shows that holiness depends on intent lishmah, and urges baking matzos oneself, with kavanah and joy, and eating such matzos all Pesach, since the same holy names are in them as in Egypt.

en: In the thirty days before Pesach Hashem takes the Jews out of the klipah of Mitzrayim little by little, and one must prepare to be taken out.
Before Moshiach the Jews will fall into the fiftieth gate of impurity, and with the power of Torah they can be brought out of it.
Pesach, whose penalty for chametz is kares, is the foundation of the Yamim Tovim and binds a Jew to Hashem; it is the time of emunah, and matzah is the food of emunah.
A sofer who writes lishmah is Hashem's messenger; the holiness comes from Hashem, which is why the sofer may not sit on one bench with the sefer Torah he wrote.
Matzos baked lishmah with kavanah, dveikus and joy by G-d-fearing people are not the same as matzos baked without kavanah, even if one fulfils the obligation with those.
The same holy names that were in the matzah the Jews ate in Egypt are in the matzah today, so one can say 'ha lachma anya'.

title.en: Thirty days of leaving Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chesed L'Avraham that from Purim, thirty days before Pesach, Hashem takes the Jews out of the klipah of Mitzrayim a little each day, and explains Mitzrayim as 'meitzar yam', what holds back the fifty gates of understanding. He says one must prepare through the daily remembrance of yetzias Mitzrayim and accepting the yoke of Heaven, asking Hashem to bend the yetzer to His service.

title.en: The forty-nine gates and the fiftieth

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ohr HaChaim that the Jews fell to the forty-ninth gate of impurity in Egypt, explaining 'avadim hayinu' as bondage to the klipah, and that before Moshiach they will fall into the fiftieth gate, from which Torah can bring them out. He reads the rasha of the Haggadah as one in the fiftieth gate of heresy, whom the Torah still tries to pull out, and notes that yetzias Mitzrayim is mentioned fifty times in the Torah, against the fifty gates.

title.en: Pesach as the foundation of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers, in the name of his rebbe, why the Torah mentions yetzias Mitzrayim more than fifty times: only fifty are in praise. He then explains with the Chiddushei HaRim that Pesach, whose penalty is kares, is the foundation that binds a Jew to Hashem, the time of emunah, recommends Shomer Emunim to those who feel weak in emunah, and calls matzah the food of emunah, like a vitamin a doctor prescribes.

title.en: The sofer as Hashem's messenger

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why a sofer may not sit on one bench with the sefer Torah he wrote, and answers that writing lishmah makes him Hashem's messenger, so the holiness comes from Hashem. The same holds for tefillin, mezuzos and tzitzis, so one should seek out a G-d-fearing sofer and spend money on it, and he describes how in Skver the tzitzis are made by hand by carefully chosen people, since a machine cannot have intent.

title.en: Baking matzos lishmah oneself

summary.en: The Mashgiach urges going to bake matzos oneself, since the holiness of the matzah comes from the kavanah, and describes baking with joy and repeating 'lishmah'. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar on the generation of the tower, contrasts a bochur who bakes after davening and mikveh with workers who bake while chatting, and explains that those who permit machine matzos rely on Rishonim who require only guarding lishmah, which is not a hiddur.

title.en: Hiddur matzos all Pesach and 'ha lachma anya'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that, following the Chasam Sofer and others, eating matzah all of Pesach is a mitzvah, compares it to the sukkah, and so recommends eating the chaburah's matzos the whole Yom Tov. He explains 'ha lachma anya': the same holy names are in today's matzah as in Egypt, the physical matzah being only an envelope, and closes by urging preparation and kavanah in the thirty days.

catalogTitle: צד ב: מעלות פסח כמו מעלת ימי הבחרות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Pesach and Nissan are the beginning of the bond with Hashem and must be guarded with every stringency, and that a person's years as a bachur are his own Nissan.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the stringencies of Pesach: chametz is forbidden even in the smallest amount, and the Ba'al HaTanya writes that on Pesach one should be stringent even for a single opinion among the Rishonim. The reason is that Pesach is a beginning, when Jews left Egypt and became a nation, and a beginning must be firm. The physical world shows the same: growth begins in Nissan, as the blessing on blossoming trees shows. In a person's life, his years as a bachur are his Nissan. Then Hashem gives unearned gifts, a light in learning and davening, as a chassan sends gifts at the start of a bond, and as the night of the Seder brings a great light. So a bachur must guard himself like Pesach, since an hour then is worth years later. The Mashgiach brings the Avnei Nezer on the worth of Nissan, and the Imrei Emes crying out a passuk for the hearts of the bachurim, and closes with a brachah.

en: Pesach carries special stringencies because it is a beginning, and a beginning must be firm and entirely good.
Nissan is the beginning of growth both in the physical world and in Jewish history, when Jews became a nation.
In a person's life, the years as a bachur are his Nissan, the time when he forms himself and his future image.
Hashem gives unearned gifts at the beginning of the bond, as a chassan sends gifts, and as the Seder night brings a great light.
A bachur must guard himself with every stringency, as a Jew does on Pesach, because a moment in those years is worth years later.

title.en: Why Pesach has so many stringencies

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how the Yamim Tovim ascend from Pesach, and the special stringencies of Pesach, citing the Ba'al HaTanya that one should be stringent even for a single opinion. He explains that Pesach is the beginning, when Jews became a nation, and a beginning must be firm.

title.en: Nissan as the start of growth and of the bond

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that growth begins in Nissan, as the blessing on blossoming trees shows, and that Nissan is a time without full completeness, like a bachur. He explains the unearned gifts of that time by a chassan sending gifts at the start of a bond, bringing a teshuvah about a broken shidduch, and the great light of the Seder night.

title.en: The years of bachurus are Nissan

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the idea to a bachur, who must guard himself like Pesach since then he forms his future. He brings a letter that an hour in those years is worth years, the Avnei Nezer on the worth of time in Nissan, and the Imrei Emes crying out a passuk for the bachurim's hearts, and closes with a brachah.

catalogTitle: ט”ו בשבט Ushers in the Months of חסד (A Deeper Understanding of the צירופי החודש)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains through the twelve arrangements of the Shem Havaya that Tu B'Shvat is the point where the din of the winter is sweetened and the months of chesed begin.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach compares the Torah to a field whose flowers hide gold and diamonds below, and sets out to dig beneath the surface of Tu B'Shvat. Each month is an arrangement of the four letters of the Shem Havaya: the Yud and Vav are masculine and chesed, the two Heis feminine and din. When the masculine letter comes first, chesed sweetens din; when the feminine comes first, din dominates, as with Esav, who put his wives before his sons. Nissan and Tishrei begin the summer and winter, while Tammuz and Teves are fully or partly reversed. Their din spills into Av and Shevat until the fifteenth, when the order turns back to chesed. From Tu B'Shvat on, the gates of chesed are open until Shavuos. The gematria of seraf (580) and ilan (91) shows the side of tumah being raised into kedushah, and the Mashgiach ties the day to davening for an esrog.

en: Each of the twelve months is a different arrangement of the four letters of the Shem Havaya.
The Yud and Vav are masculine and chesed, the Heis feminine and din; when the masculine comes first, chesed sweetens din.
Tammuz and Teves are reversed arrangements of din, and their din spills into Av and Shevat until the fifteenth of the month.
From Tu B'Shvat until Shavuos the gates of chesed are open, and these days are meant to be used for Torah and avodah.
Seraf (580) rising into the ilan (91) shows the power of tumah being raised and absorbed into kedushah.
On Tu B'Shvat one davens for the esrog, and the berachah on fruit is said with the 'pri etz hadar' in mind.

candidateTopics: arrangements of the Shem Havaya for each month
months of chesed from Tu B'Shvat to Shavuos

title.en: Digging beneath the surface; the Shem Havaya

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the levels of Torah to a field of flowers with gold and diamonds below, and introduces the idea that each month is an arrangement of the Shem Havaya. He presents its letters as father, mother, son and daughter, the masculine being chesed and the feminine din.

title.en: Giver and receiver: chassan and kallah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the chassan, chesed, gives and the kallah, din, receives, which is why kiddushin and the kesubah go only from him to her. He shows that the Yud and Vav are masculine letters and the Hei feminine, as in women's names, and that the four letters with two identical Heis give twelve arrangements, one per month.

title.en: In kedushah the masculine comes first

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that Yaakov put his sons before his wives while Esav did the reverse, and explains that the right side is chesed: we write from right to left and start with the right hand. He adds examples from the nations, from white and red, and from Achashverosh, whose deference to his wife brought him trouble.

title.en: Nissan and Tishrei, kings of the year

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows in the siddur that each month has its arrangement and a passuk it comes from. Nissan, the pleasant month of spring, is Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei in order, from the roshei teivos of 'Yismechu hashamayim', while Tishrei, king of the winter months, comes from the Aleph-Beis backwards and turns to chesed in its second half through the avodah of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.

title.en: Tammuz, Teves, and the turn on the fifteenth

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Tammuz, the peak of summer, has the Shem entirely backwards, from sofei teivos, which is why the meraglim's journey and the churban began then, and its din lasts into Av until the fifteenth. Likewise Teves, the brunt of winter, is reversed and its din spills into Shevat, whose first half is Hei-Yud and second half Vav-Hei, sweetened from Tu B'Shvat.

title.en: Having the arrangement in mind without mechanical davening

summary.en: The Mashgiach discusses the sefarim's advice to have the month's arrangement in mind, warning that thinking only of letters makes davening mechanical, as Rebbe Nachman of Breslov said. Only if it truly lifts one's davening, drawing down chesed and connecting to Hashem, should one do it; in a month like Tammuz one sweetens the din by connecting to chesed.

title.en: From Tu B'Shvat to Shavuos: the gates of chesed

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Divrei Chaim's observation that from Tu B'Shvat to Shavuos there are never two weeks without a Yom Tov, an ascent of growing chesed in which the gates are open and should be used for Torah and avodah. He describes the sap already rising in the roots though nothing is yet seen on the tree.

title.en: Havaya and Adnus: the union in the Mikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Shem Havaya is chesed and the Shem Adnus din, the chassan and kallah, and their union is the union of Hakadosh Baruch Hu and Knesses Yisrael, whose seat is the Mikdash. He notes the passuk read the day before and the siddurim that join the two Names, then says that tumah mirrors kedushah with its own masculine and feminine, where the feminine dominates.

title.en: The two forces of tumah and the number 580

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ohr HaChaim in Vayechi, who saw the power of tumah as two dogs, male and female, and overcame the male at once but the female only with difficulty. He explains that the two names of tumah together equal 580, the number of Esav's gift animals and of Seir, while Havaya and Adnus together equal 91, the gematria of Amen.

title.en: Seraf in the ilan; davening for the esrog

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Rashi's phrase that on Tu B'Shvat the seraf rises in the ilan as 580 being raised into 91: the power of tumah sublimated into kedushah, as Nissan, Purim and Pesach approach. He ties the day to davening for the esrog, brings the Bnei Yissaschar and the custom to say borei pri ha'etz and perhaps shehecheyanu, and gives a remez that the berachah is said with the 'pri etz hadar' in mind.

title.en: Barren trees, and only scratching the surface

summary.en: The Mashgiach repeats from the day before Rashi's explanation that barren trees will one day give fruit, since all trees were created fruitful before Adam's sin, and says this is a time to daven for them. He closes that all these insights only scratch the surface, a drop in the ocean of what Tu B'Shvat is, until Moshiach comes.

catalogTitle: צד א: פסח - יו"ט של עשיית המצוות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Pesach, the head of all the festivals and the yom tov of Avraham Avinu, is the time of emunah, which a Jew draws into himself through the mitzvos of the yom tov and above all through matzah baked with heart, while the events of the day call for preparing seriously for Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that each Pesach and each Shabbos is greater than the one before: the generations are lower, but because they are so low they can raise sparks the earlier generations could not reach, and bodies become ever more refined. That is why mitzvos, done with the body, are in this respect greater than Torah. Nissan is full of physical preparation, and Pesach, the yom tov of Avraham, is the root of the festivals. Turning to the war of the day, he relates traditions of tzaddikim about the nations being dragged into war before Moshiach and urges serious preparation, so as not to spoil the moment. He then shows, through the two reasons given for Shabbos, that yetzias Mitzrayim reveals the ten sayings of creation and is the root of emunah. Every Jew inherits emunah from Avraham; Pesach and matzah, the food of faith, bring it into the open, so the matzah should be baked by sincere Jews with heart, not mechanically.

en: Each Pesach and Shabbos is greater than the last, because the low generations before Moshiach can raise sparks from a place the earlier generations never reached.
The soul needs no repair; it came down to refine the body, which is why mitzvos, done with the body, are in this respect greater than Torah study.
Pesach is the head of all the festivals and the yom tov of Avraham Avinu; through it a Jew binds himself to the root, to emunah.
Yetzias Mitzrayim revealed openly the ten powers of creation that no one saw, and so it is the root of emunah.
Every Jew has emunah by inheritance from Avraham; Torah, mitzvos and Pesach bring the hidden faith into the open.
Matzah is the food of faith; it should be baked by sincere Jews with heart and joy, and a mitzvah should not be done mechanically.

matzah as the food of faith
ikvesa d'meshicha and the war before Moshiach
mitzvos with the body versus torah

title.en: Lower generations, greater refinement

summary.en: The Mashgiach says each Pesach and Shabbos is greater than the last: the late generations are so low that they can raise sparks from the fiftieth gate, and bodies grow more refined. Since the soul came down only to refine the body, he explains with the Tanya why mitzvos are in this respect greater than Torah.

title.en: Pesach, head of the festivals

summary.en: Nissan is full of physical preparation, and Pesach is the head of all the festivals. The Mashgiach brings the Chiddushei HaRim that the kares of Pesach shows it binds a Jew to the root, and explains that Pesach is Avraham's yom tov, just as the blessing is Magen Avraham, while Magen David belongs to the time of Moshiach.

title.en: Not a time for jokes: the war before Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach says joking has become a klipah in Chassidus, and that this is a serious time: the Midrash says war between kingdoms heralds Moshiach. He relates a tradition passed down from Reb Mottele of Slonim that before Moshiach the nations will be dragged into war against their will, and applies it to the war in Iraq.

title.en: Tzaddikim foresee; preparing seriously

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the tradition was meant to be passed on: to strengthen Jews when they would be frightened. He tells of the Stoliner Rebbe's prediction about Russia and of the Bluzhever Rav, who turned pale at a joke that Moshiach had come because he was not yet ready, and calls for approaching this Pesach very seriously.

title.en: From Purim to erev Pesach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the war on Amalek begins on Purim and ends on erev Pesach, and the Avnei Nezer on why the main Purim seudah is held at night, noting that the war began on Purim night. He warns not to spoil the moment, and introduces the series of talks he will build on the Nesivos Shalom until Pesach.

title.en: Creation and the Exodus: one testimony

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how the two reasons for Shabbos in the two Luchos, creation and yetzias Mitzrayim, belong together. With the Chiddushei HaRim and the Arizal he shows that the ten plagues mirror the ten sayings of creation in reverse, so the Exodus revealed what was hidden at creation and is the root of emunah; Pesach is the yom tov of emunah.

title.en: Inherited faith and the food of faith

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew, even a sinner, believes by inheritance from Avraham, and that there is no true Jewish heretic, only a coating. Torah, mitzvos and Pesach bring this faith into the open, and matzah, called the food of faith in the Zohar, carries holy names into the body.

title.en: Simplicity, not mechanical kavanos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rebbe Reb Elimelech and Rav Tzadok that one should serve Hashem simply and not with calculated kavanos, which make a mitzvah mechanical, as with a shofar blower watching the second hand. He describes a matzah bakery he saw and says matzah should be baked by sincere Jews with kavanah and joy.

title.en: Matzah as a sign; emunah the foundation

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Tosafos that matzah is the sign of Pesach in place of tefillin, and the view that eating matzah all of Pesach is a mitzvah, compared to sukkah. He closes that emunah is a Jew's dearest possession and the foundation of all mitzvos, and that Pesach, the root of the festivals, deserves more care than any other yom tov.

catalogTitle: צד ב: דצ"ך עד"ש באח"ב בגימטרי' ישמעאלים (עניני דיומא במלחמה באירק)

oneLiner.en: During the war in Iraq before Pesach, the Mashgiach calls for tefillah for the Jewish soldiers, explains that today's Arabs of Iraq are Bavel and Yishmael, and shows that Rabbi Yehuda's simanim d'tzach adash b'achav equal 'Yishmaelim' in gematria.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a phone call from an army chaplain: over a thousand Jewish soldiers are now in Iraq as the battle for Baghdad begins, and he calls on everyone to daven for them and for the geulah. Iraq is Bavel, by the rivers Pras and Chidekel where the Jews sat and wept, and its Arabs, who identify with Bavel, carry the din of Bavel. He brings Dovid Hamelech's blessing on whoever repays Bavel and the duty to pray for the welfare of the kingdom, especially America, a kingdom of kindness. The Yishmaelim began galus Mitzrayim by selling Yosef; therefore at the Seder one pours wine at d'tzach adash b'achav, which equals Yishmaelim, drawing judgment on them. He contrasts Edom and Yishmael, then teaches that any Jew may have his hour, as the boy's whistle in the Ba'al Shem Tov's story showed, and stresses the power of the first twelve days of Nissan and of minhag Yisrael, before closing with Pesach preparation.

en: The Mashgiach says one is obligated to daven for the Jewish soldiers fighting in Iraq, and that the war should bring the geulah.
The Arabs of Iraq identify with Bavel and therefore have the din of Bavel, just as those who present themselves as a nation receive its din.
There is a mitzvah to pray for the welfare of the government one lives under, especially America, which has never persecuted or expelled Jews.
Rabbi Yehuda's simanim d'tzach adash b'achav equal 'Yishmaelim' in gematria; pouring wine there draws judgment on the Yishmaelim, who began galus Mitzrayim.
Every Jew has his hour, when a single heartfelt tefillah or moment of teshuvah can accomplish more than the greatest tzaddik of the generation.
The first twelve days of Nissan, when the Nesiim are read, have the power to subdue the twelve princes of Yishmael, and a minhag Yisrael can be stronger than a halachah.

candidateTopics: galus Mitzrayim and the sale of Yosef

title.en: Jewish soldiers in Iraq and the call to daven

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a call from an army chaplain who reported over a thousand Jewish soldiers in Iraq as the battle for Baghdad begins. He explains why the enemy's name is not mentioned, citing the Bnei Yissaschar, and says one is obligated to daven for the soldiers and for the geulah the war should bring.

title.en: By the rivers of Bavel

summary.en: The Mashgiach points out that the war is taking place by the rivers Pras and Chidekel, the rivers of Bavel. He describes the Babylonian ruler who saw himself as a new Nevuchadnetzar and fired missiles at Eretz Yisrael, and recalls the Jews who sat by these rivers in galus and refused to play the songs of Zion.

title.en: The Arabs as Bavel; praying for America

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Arabs of Iraq identify with Bavel and so have its din, bringing Rashi on the king of Arad and a Midrash that the Babylonians will be revived to receive their punishment. He cites Dovid Hamelech's blessing on whoever repays Bavel, and the mitzvah to pray for the government, especially America, a kingdom of kindness.

title.en: Yishmael began galus Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that galus Mitzrayim began with the sale of Yosef to the Yishmaelim, citing Targum Yonasan. He brings from the Chofetz Chaim that the angels above speak of a person as Jews speak of him below, so arousing merit on Jews and judgment on the wicked has effect in Heaven.

title.en: D'tzach adash b'achav equals Yishmaelim

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Rabbi Yehuda's simanim are recited at the Seder, explains that wine has the power to draw kindness to Jews and judgment to their enemies, and reveals that d'tzach adash b'achav equals Yishmaelim in gematria. He contrasts Edom, from whom converts come, with Yishmael, from whom none come, and links the two to se'or and chametz.

title.en: Every Jew has his hour

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that no one knows how much his learning and davening can accomplish, bringing the Mishnah that every person has his hour and the Ba'al Shem Tov's story of the simple boy whose whistle on Yom Kippur annulled a decree. He adds Rashi's 'when the fox has its hour' and the Gemara that a person should see the world as half meritorious and half guilty.

title.en: The twelve days of Nissan and the power of minhag

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the days of Nissan as a time when the world is renewed, and brings Targum Yonasan that the twelve Nesiim's offerings subdue the twelve princes of Yishmael. Though reading the Nesiim in Nissan is only a minhag, he explains that minhag Yisrael carries the prophecy of Klal Yisrael, citing the Kuzari and the minhag of Hallel on Rosh Chodesh.

title.en: Removing the world's chametz; Rosh Chodesh Nissan

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Yishmael's name may be mentioned though it is forbidden to name a rasha, since it is written in the Torah. He describes the pre-Pesach cleaning as burning the world's chametz, Yishmael and Amalek, urges learning in every free moment, and closes with the Ba'al Shem Tov on Rosh Chodesh Nissan as the Rosh Hashanah for kings and wishes for Pesach in Yerushalayim.

catalogTitle: דרוש בענין: מעשה ברבי אליעזר וכו' ובני בניו של המן שלמדו תורה בבני ברק

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains how Timna's desire to cling to the family of Avraham survived, hidden and untouched, through Amalek and Haman until it produced Haman's descendants who learned Torah in Bnei Brak, and how the Tannaim of the Haggadah came there to repair them.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Sfas Emes on the Tannaim in Bnei Brak who lost track of time, and with the question why Amalek was only weakened. He then takes up the Gemara that Haman's descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak, though no convert may be accepted from Amalek. The answer lies in Timna: her desire to join the family of Avraham was a real bond, and since she came to Elifaz only as a pilegesh, her line passed through Amalek like an insulated wire without becoming Amalek. Haman's joy at Esther's feast freed that spark, which became Rav Shmuel bar Shilas. Shaul's sparing of Agag and Moshe's lowered hands left a remnant for Purim. The people of Bnei Brak struggled with the morning Krias Shema, a flaw from Zeresh, and the Tannaim, sharing their flaw by missing the matzah, repaired them. He closes with Birkas Hachama on erev Pesach and the power of a Jew's desire.

en: Timna's desire to cling to the family of Avraham was a sign of a real bond, and a good desire is never lost.
Because Timna began as a pilegesh, with no true bond, her line only passed through Amalek, so the ban on accepting converts from Amalek did not apply to Haman's descendants who came from her.
Amalek was deliberately not wiped out, by Moshe's lowered hands and by Shaul sparing Agag, so that Purim and Haman's righteous descendants could come about.
The Tannaim came to Bnei Brak to repair Haman's descendants, who could not properly say the morning Krias Shema.
The Mashgiach says one must daven to have a desire for Torah, tefillah and mitzvos, since Pesach is the time of desire.

candidateTopics: Haggadah: the Tannaim in Bnei Brak
Timna and the descendants of Haman
Rav Shmuel bar Shilas and teachers of children
Purim and the feast of Esther

title.en: Bnei Brak, Amalek and Haman's descendants

summary.en: The Mashgiach cites the Sfas Emes that the Tannaim lost track of time, asks why Amalek was only weakened, and brings Menashe's mockery of the verse about Timna. He then cites the Gemara that Haman's descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak and asks how, when no convert may be accepted from Amalek.

title.en: Timna's desire and what a pilegesh is

summary.en: Citing the Rambam that every verse is equally from Heaven, the Mashgiach explains that Timna had a desire for kedushah, that desire means clinging, and that a desire shows a real connection. A pilegesh, though, has no true bond, and as the beginning of a thing holds all of it, her tie to Elifaz stayed separate, like an insulated wire.

title.en: Timna's line passes through Amalek

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that from Timna came Amalek and Haman, and from Haman's descendants Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, the model teacher of children. Since Timna's line only passed through Amalek, the oath against converts from Amalek does not apply; he adds the Gilgulei Neshamos that Timna was reincarnated in Bilaam's donkey.

title.en: Haman's joy at Esther's feast

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Kedushas Levi and Tiferes Shlomo, who ask how Haman could feel joy, and answer that the holy feast of Esther gave him vitality, from which his righteous descendants could come. The Mashgiach adds that this freed the spark of Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, compares it to Agag fathering a child the night Shaul spared him, and notes that the feast was a Pesach meal.

title.en: Zeresh saved, and Haman's war on the moadim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Zeresh escaped: the spark destined for Haman's descendants passed through her. He reads 'yavo hamelech veHaman hayom' as holding Hashem's Name and the words 'they learned Torah in Bnei Brak', and explains that Haman hated the Yamim Tovim and the schoolchildren that sustain Klal Yisrael, while Timna, as Bilaam's donkey, spoke in favor of the three festivals.

title.en: Blessing Haman on Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that one must drink on Purim until he cannot tell 'blessed Mordechai' from 'cursed Haman', and the Arizal that a blessing said on Haman by mistake goes only to the spark of holiness in him. The same holds for Zeresh, from whom came Shilas, the mother of Rav Shmuel bar Shilas.

title.en: Why Agag and Amalek were left alive

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Shmuel never rebuked Shaul for sparing Agag, and brings the Ruzhiner: by leaving Agag, from whom Haman came, Shaul brought Purim to the world. This also explains why Moshe lowered his hands and Amalek was only weakened, so that a remnant would stay until Moshiach ben Yosef; Haman fought the moadim and the schoolchildren, the two things that come from Timna.

title.en: Bnei Brak's struggle with Krias Shema

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the people of Bnei Brak, descendants of Haman, struggled with the morning Krias Shema, as many people today complain they cannot concentrate on it. This was a flaw from Zeresh, who sought to stop Mordechai's morning Krias Shema, and a gentile's flaw passes to his descendants even after conversion; Amalek also had a hold on the tribe of Dan, in whose land Bnei Brak lay, so the sages came from the Galil to help them.

title.en: Why the Tannaim missed the matzah

summary.en: Returning to the Sfas Emes, the Mashgiach asks how Hashem let the great Tannaim miss eating matzah on Pesach night, and explains that the telling of the Exodus takes a Jew out of all his troubles, which made the night right for helping the people of Bnei Brak. He then develops that at a great success something must be given to the Sitra Achra, like the se'ir la'azazel, mayim acharonim and kaparos, and suggests that the fast on Pesach in Esther's time was such an appeasement for the Purim miracle.

title.en: The Tannaim repair Haman's descendants

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings from the Ba'al Shem Tov that a tzaddik can only lift a sinner if he has some share in the sin, and explains that the Tannaim, by not eating matzah as the Jews could not in Haman's time, gained that share and freed Haman's descendants to say Krias Shema. He returns to the Rambam that the verse about Timna equals Shema Yisrael, and concludes with the power of a Jew's desire.

title.en: Birkas Hachama: the sun belongs to Yaakov

summary.en: The Mashgiach turns to the year's Birkas Hachama, approached with great desire. He explains that Hashem gave the sun, nature, to Esav and the moon to Yaakov, yet in truth everything belongs to Yisrael, and only in this world does Esav seem to hold nature, as Yerushalayim is written without a yud during the exile.

title.en: The sun's return, erev Pesach, and desire

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that when the sun returns to its first point, as before the sin, it is revealed that the world was made for Yisrael, and Birkas Hachama comforts the sun that it will return to Yaakov. A Birkas Hachama on erev Pesach is greater, since the war against Amalek, Shaul's war with Agag and that of Moshiach ben Yosef, is erev Pesach. He closes that Pesach is desire, that Timna's desire survived until Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, and with a tefillah for the coming of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: A Coin of Fire

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the half-shekel is a 'coin of fire', the yud of Hashem's Name and the indestructible point in every Jew, and that this is why it defeated Haman's shekalim and why Yehoash is its haftarah.

abstract.en: For Parshas Shekalim the Mashgiach asks why the half-shekel was the merit that saved the Jews from Haman. He starts from Rashi's 'coin of fire' and a vort that a talmid of Rebbe Reb Bunim heard in Germany: Hashem wants the fire within a mitzvah, not its metal. The Alshich's reading of the apiryon shows the Beis Hamikdash was precious for the love inside it. Avraham's 400 shekalim for Me'aras HaMachpelah were compounded above, while Efron, named from afar (earth), kept cold metal. The four parshiyos match the four letters of Hashem's Name, and Shekalim is the yud, fire. The haftarah's Yehoash, whose soul came from shekalim, killed Zechariah on Yom Kippur in the Mikdash, forgetting a kindness as Haman did. Yet shekalim is the indestructible point in every Jew, where all are equal as children; it outweighed Haman's shekalim, and through it Yehoash too will be atoned.

en: The coin of fire Hashem showed Moshe teaches that what counts in a mitzvah is the fire and devotion within it, not its outward material.
A gift given with love is multiplied as it rises; Avraham's 400 shekalim for Me'aras HaMachpelah were registered above as endless sums.
The four parshiyos correspond to the four letters of the Shem Havayah, and Shekalim is the yud, the source of fire.
Every Jew's neshama comes from a particular mitzvah, and Yehoash, who renewed the mitzvah of shekalim, has a neshama from shekalim.
Shekalim is the kotzo shel yud, the nucleus in every Jew that no aveirah can destroy, and in its merit the Jews could not be annihilated in Haman's time.
In shekalim rich and poor give alike because it touches the root where Jews are Hashem's children, all equally His, as on Yom Kippur.

title.en: Parshas Shekalim and the coin of fire

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces the four parshiyos and the Gemara that the Jews' shekalim came before Haman's ten thousand talents of silver. He then asks what 'this they shall give' means and brings Rashi that Hashem showed Moshe a coin of fire from under the Heavenly Throne.

title.en: The vort heard in Germany

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a talmid of Rebbe Reb Bunim who heard a German preacher say that Hashem wants a coin of fire, the warmth and devotion that go with a mitzvah. He applies this to tefillin, tzitzis and tefillah, notes that shekel equals nefesh in gematria, and brings Rebbe Reb Bunim's explanation that the German Jews merited this vort through their hachnasas orchim.

title.en: The glowing love inside the Beis Hamikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Alshich on the apiryon of Shir Hashirim: Hashem lacks no silver or gold, and what He wanted in the Beis Hamikdash was the glowing love of the Jews inside it. He contrasts a cold Roman edifice and a bronze statue with living people who have a neshama.

title.en: Avraham's compounded shekalim

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what the Musaf piyut of Parshas Shekalim means by asking Hashem to remember the shekalim of Efron. A dollar given with love is multiplied as it rises, and Avraham, who knew the holiness of Me'aras HaMachpelah, gave his 400 shekalim with such love that they were registered above as endless sums.

title.en: Fire, earth and the yud of Hashem's Name

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the four elements, fire rising and earth falling. Efron, named for afar, kept only cold metal while Avraham's fire went up, and 'Machpelah' means compounding. The four parshiyos correspond to the four letters of the Shem Havayah, and Shekalim is the yud, the fire.

title.en: Yehoash and the mitzvah of shekalim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the haftarah tells how King Yehoash renewed the forgotten mitzvah of shekalim. Every Jew's neshama comes from a particular mitzvah, as with a tzaddik who dealt with his sukkah every day of the year, so Yehoash's neshama comes from shekalim.

title.en: Yehoash in the Kodesh HaKadashim and Zechariah's death

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Yehoash, the last of the house of David, was hidden in the Kodesh HaKadashim for six years and crowned at seven. Later his servants made him a deity, and he killed Zechariah, the Kohen Gadol and Navi, on Yom Kippur in the Mikdash, forgetting Yehoyada's kindness; Zechariah's blood boiled until the Churban.

title.en: Like Haman: Kodesh HaKadashim defiled

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares Yehoash to Haman, who did not remember Shaul's mercy to Agag. Using Sefer Yetzirah's three dimensions of world, year and soul, he shows that Yehoash killed the Kohen Gadol, the Kodesh HaKadashim of souls, in the holiest place on the holiest day.

title.en: The kotzo shel yud and the indestructible nucleus

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the small mitzvah of shekalim saved the Jews from Haman. Shekalim is the yud, and the yud has a kotz, the nucleus; every Jew has an indestructible point, like the luz bone, from which he is rebuilt however deep he falls.

title.en: One root of all Jews

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that shekalim corresponds to that nucleus, so in its merit the Jews, who cannot be totally destroyed, were saved. He brings the Chasam Sofer that all Jews share one root to which teshuvah returns, his reading of the passuk comparing Jews to the children of Kush, and the future circle dance where every point is equally close to the center.

title.en: Equal half-shekalim: children, not servants

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts other mitzvos, which each Jew performs on his own level, with shekalim, where rich and poor give the same. Shekalim, called the money of atonement, belongs to Yom Kippur, the day of the circle dance and of forgiveness, where Jews are children and not servants, and where the lot chooses without a reason, as with Purim.

title.en: Haman's shekalim against ours; Yehoash is not Haman

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the Jews' shekalim came before Haman's: theirs are fire, the yud, given with the joy of Adar, while Haman's are earth. Yehoash fits the haftarah because, though guilty of Haman's crime, his neshama of shekalim cannot be destroyed, which shows every Jew that he can never be lost forever.

title.en: The rising fire and the gates of mercy

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that even today the eagerness for the mitzvah of shekalim is fire that rises to the heavenly Beis Hamikdash. He finds a hint that Yom Kippur will atone for Yehoash, who came from the Kodesh HaKadashim, and closes with the Gemara on Mordechai ben Yair ben Shimi ben Kish, who knocked on the gates of mercy that open on Yom Kippur and Purim.

catalogTitle: ביאור מצות פדיון פטר חמור: לב טוב' אמונה' ופשטות

oneLiner.en: Through the mitzvah of redeeming the firstborn donkey, the Mashgiach shows that the klipah of Mitzrayim is a begrudging eye, that the donkey's holiness is its simplicity, and that the generation before Moshiach brings the geulah through simple emunah and a good heart toward others.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the two mitzvos of the firstborn donkey, redemption and breaking its neck, and asks for whom the second was given at all. He then asks why the verse about borrowing from the Egyptians appears inside Moshe's warning of makas bechoros. Using Rashi's two reasons for the mitzvah and the Arizal's teaching that Egypt's root is tzaras ayin, a begrudging eye, he explains that makas bechoros broke that root, so the Egyptians could now give with good will. The donkey that carried the wealth with a good eye earned redemption; a stingy owner is sent a donkey that must be destroyed, purifying his own trait. With the Maharal he explains the donkey's virtue as simplicity, like matzah, and its flaw as laziness, absent in the special donkey of Avraham, Moshe and Moshiach. Our simple generation's task is emunah peshutah, together with goodwill toward every Jew, which will bring Moshiach on his donkey.

en: According to the Arizal, the root klipah of Mitzrayim is tzaras ayin: an inability to give to or begrudge good to anyone else.
Makas bechoros struck the root of Egypt and broke its tzaras ayin, which is why the borrowing from the Egyptians, given with chen, belongs inside the warning of that plague.
A man's soul extends into his possessions, so a stingy owner's trait enters his firstborn donkey, and breaking its neck weakens the trait in him.
Following the Maharal, the donkey's virtue is simplicity, a spiritual virtue like that of matzah and the Kohen Gadol's white garments, while its flaw is laziness.
The generation before Moshiach has no great attainments; its particular mitzvah is simple emunah, and that emunah gives strength to Moshiach's donkey to come.
Pesach, the Yom Tov of emunah and of chesed, is the time to break the klipah of Mitzrayim by begrudging no one, including other Chassidim and other Rebbes.

title.en: Two mitzvos of the firstborn donkey

summary.en: After thanking the Stoliner chevra, the Mashgiach recalls the morning's reading of Kadesh li kol bechor and the two mitzvos of the firstborn donkey, redemption and breaking its neck. He asks for whom the mitzvah of breaking the neck was given, since an honest Jew redeems and one who disobeys would not break the neck either.

title.en: Borrowing inside the warning of makas bechoros

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through the verses of Moshe's last warning to Pharaoh, which Rashi says was said while still standing before him, and notes that the command to borrow from the Egyptians and the chen they were given are inserted in the middle. He asks why this appears twice and what borrowing has to do with makas bechoros.

title.en: Rashi's two reasons and Egypt's begrudging eye

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi's two reasons why only the donkey among impure animals has this mitzvah: Egypt is compared to donkeys, and the donkeys helped carry out the wealth. He suggests one reason fits redemption and the other breaking the neck, then brings the Arizal that Egypt's root is tzaras ayin, as the Gemara says even the nations' kindness is for themselves.

title.en: Matzah, free fish, and the broken root of Egypt

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that the Egyptians fed the Jews matzah so they would eat little, and the Midrash on the fish eaten 'for free', both showing Egypt could not give. He explains that makas bechoros broke Egypt's angel and root, so its tzaras ayin was nullified and the Egyptians gave with chen, a free gift; this is why the borrowing is part of the warning.

title.en: The soul extends into one's possessions

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the donkey, though linked to Egypt, helped with a good eye and so earned redemption. From the Pri Tzaddik he brings that a person's soul extends into his property, illustrated by Rebbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey that would not eat untithed food; a stingy owner's trait enters his donkey, and destroying it weakens the klipah, like Moshe grinding the egel.

title.en: Seeing the kedushah in one's produce

summary.en: Returning to his opening question, the Mashgiach brings from the Divrei Yisrael, in the name of Rebbi Yechezkel of Kuzmir, that in Temple times a Jew could see in his field how much of the produce held the kedushah of terumah, a fortieth, a fiftieth or a sixtieth. In the same way a good-eyed Jew sees holiness in his firstborn donkey and redeems it, while a stingy one is sent a donkey carrying Egypt's klipah, and breaking its neck purifies his heart, like burning chametz.

title.en: The donkey of Avraham, Moshe and Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that Moshe rode the special donkey created at twilight, the same one Avraham took to the Akeidah and on which Moshiach will come. He asks why the donkey alone of the impure animals has kedushah and answers with the Maharal: the donkey is chomer, utterly simple, and simplicity, with nothing mixed in, is a spiritual virtue close to Hashem, while the horse's pride and beauty is only a physical one.

title.en: Matzah, white garments and simple Jews

summary.en: Continuing the Maharal, the Mashgiach explains that matzah is holy because it is simple flour and water without the added work of time, and that the Kohen Gadol entered the Kodesh HaKodashim in plain white garments. He tells how the Ruzhiner refused a communal leader's offer to keep simple Jews out of the town shul, saying his forebears were all simple Jews.

title.en: Simplicity with zrizus, not laziness

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the simple donkey is nonetheless impure and answers that it is also lazy, while matzah is simplicity joined with zrizus. Using the Gemara that one running on Erev Shabbos is exempt, he explains that the donkey created at twilight on Erev Shabbos was made in haste, so the donkey of Avraham, of Moshe at the Exodus and of Moshiach has the virtue of matzah, and every donkey shares some kedushah through its kind.

title.en: A simple generation and its mitzvah of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes our generation as simple, without the Yom Kippur and Yamim Noraim of earlier generations. From the Gemara and the Tanya he brings that each person and each generation has its own mitzvah, and that the mitzvah of the generation before Moshiach is emunah, the first of the Ten Commandments, which is above understanding; even those who saw the miracles at the sea still had emunah in what lay beyond their grasp.

title.en: Simple emunah brings Moshiach's donkey

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that the redemption comes in the merit of emunah and explains that the simpler the emunah, the more strength it gives Moshiach to come on his simple donkey, like the emunah of our grandmothers. He shows the same at the Akeidah: Avraham's levels and feeling were taken from him, and he went on the donkey with simple emunah.

title.en: Temimus: every Jew and his own Rebbe

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the simple Jew who serves Hashem without politics brings Moshiach, and that a donkey, unlike a horse, never rebels against its master. Every Jew is bound to his own Rebbe or Rosh Yeshiva, but disparaging another is not temimus; he brings the Sanzer Rav on this and the Chasam Sofer's letter that Moshiach could have come in the generation of Rebbi Yaakov Emden and Rebbi Yonasan, but did not because disciples disparaged the gedolim.

title.en: Pesach: emunah, chesed and fargin

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Pesach the Yom Tov of simple emunah and of chesed, a time to break the klipah of Mitzrayim by rejoicing in another Jew's virtues, and brings that matzah, the food of emunah, brings emunah when eaten all of Pesach. He ends with a brachah for a speedy geulah; dedications and an announcement follow.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the twelve paths of Kerias Yam Suf and the twelve tones of song mark an exile still divided, while the future redemption will have only the seven tones of joy that come together in Shabbos, and he urges saying the daily Shirah with joy to bring salvation.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Mechilta: had the Jews at the sea said 'Hashem melech' instead of 'Hashem yimloch', there would have been no further exile. He asks why the sea split into twelve paths while the future sea will split into seven streams. Through Yosef, whose name points to the future redemption, he explains that the Exodus was only half a redemption, a Yachatz, and the sea split then only in Yosef's merit. He then turns to song: a niggun is a heavenly match of tones, its seven tones parallel the seven days, the seven shepherds and Shabbos, while twelve stands for division. On the piano, seven white keys of chesed and five black keys of din make twelve, the tones of exile; in the future only the seven will remain. He closes with Sefer Chareidim's six easy segulos, above all saying the Shirah daily with joy, which draws salvation for the Jews of Eretz Yisroel.

en: The Exodus and the splitting of the sea were only half of the redemption, a Yachatz; the rest of the debt of exile still has to be completed in the long galus.
The sea split for Yosef's merit, because his self-sacrifice went beyond nature, yet it stays bound to its original condition, which will be fulfilled in the days of Moshiach.
A niggun is a heavenly match of tones that fit one another, as incomprehensible as a shidduch, which is why song belongs at a wedding.
The seven tones of song parallel the seven days of creation, the seven shepherds and the seven 'kol Hashem', and Shabbos, the seventh, completes them, so Shabbos is the day of song.
Twelve, the tribes, the weekday brachos and the seven white with five black keys, is division and exile; seven, Shabbos, Yerushalayim and David, is unity and redemption.
In the future there will be only the seven tones of joy, song without weeping, and then 'Hashem melech' will be said.
Saying the Shirah daily with joy and intent is an easy segulah for atonement and draws miracles and salvation for all of Klal Yisroel.
