title.en: Sefirah and the students of Rabbi Akiva

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the students of Rabbi Akiva were punished specifically in Sefirah, and explains that these days are for preparing good middos, the vessel for receiving the Torah. He announces that in the coming weeks he will speak about improving middos between man and his fellow.

title.en: A hard word about the community's middos

summary.en: Saying it may give offense, the Mashgiach states that his community in Boro Park and Flatbush is not distinguished for good middos, and attributes this to the inhuman conditions the young survivors of the camps had to live through. Since a Jew is good by nature, he expects this foreign trait to be rejected over time, and calls for a cheshbon hanefesh in these days.

title.en: Avraham, Beis Hillel and Rachel

summary.en: The Mashgiach begins the proofs from Tanach and Chazal: the saying to be careful with a friend's honor, Avraham's hospitality right after his milah, Beis Hillel who always quoted Beis Shammai first, and Rachel who gave Leah the signs so she would not be shamed, in whose merit the children return.

title.en: Yosef, Tomer Devorah and respect for every creature

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows how Yosef sent everyone out so his brothers would not be shamed, brings the Tomer Devorah that one must respect every creature since Hashem made it with wisdom, and the Gemara that Rebbi's suffering ended through his mercy on small animals. He adds that shaming someone in public costs one's share in the World to Come, and that one who causes pain must ask forgiveness even after paying.

title.en: Esav's cry and Boaz's sixty children

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that even Yaakov, who caused Esav to cry out, remained in debt until the cry of Mordechai generations later, and brings the Zohar about Esav's tears. He then tells the Gemara that Boaz lost his sixty children because he never invited the childless Manoach to his weddings.

title.en: Honor even for a stone, a tree and a sinner

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that the Torah guards the honor of the mizbe'ach's stones with a ramp, hides which tree was the Etz HaDa'as so it should not be shamed, sends home all exempt soldiers to cover for the sinner, killed Bilam's donkey for Bilam's honor, and lowers the thief's payment when he carried a sheep. From here he argues one must not jump to accuse and shame people.

title.en: The plague that hides, and the chol bird

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that a plague which takes mamzerim takes others with them so no family is singled out, and the Midrash that the chol bird in Noach's ark did not ask for food so as not to burden Noach, and was blessed to live forever. He notes that a bird's good nature is a lesson for people.

title.en: Tamar and the wife of Potiphar: two Moshiachs

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that the story of Tamar is placed next to that of Potiphar's wife because both acted for the sake of Heaven, and explains that the two parshiyos speak of the two Moshiachs, ben David from Yehudah and Tamar and ben Yosef from Yosef. He describes how Tamar, knowing Moshiach would come from her, still would not name Yehudah when taken to be burned.

title.en: Potiphar's wife, Osnas and Shaul

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Potiphar's wife, who also meant to bring Moshiach but had Yosef thrown into prison when he refused, with Tamar, and concludes that the difference was good middos; she merited nothing, as Osnas was only her adopted daughter, the daughter of Dinah. He adds that Shaul merited kingship because he spoke of his servant as an equal.

title.en: Worse than taking one's own life

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why one who takes his own life loses his share in the World to Come: death itself atones for a person, but here the death is the sin. Even so, he concludes, Tamar chose to be burned rather than shame Yehudah, so shaming another in public is graver still.

title.en: Two stories of the Bluzhever Rebbe

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Bluzhever Rebbe, who told the king's doctor that six days before Matan Torah a Jewish heart cannot beat normally, and of the responsum of his grandfather, the Tzvi LaTzaddik, forbidding even passive self-destruction, which later saved the Rebbe in the camps when he decided to eat his bread.

title.en: The poor man's bird with its feathers

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why a bird offering is burned with its feathers despite their foul smell, and brings Chazal that it is so the mizbe'ach be adorned with the poor man's korban. He applies this to a small gift at a simcha and to a simple answer in learning, which one must welcome and praise.

title.en: Different faces, different minds

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Chazal that as faces differ so do opinions, explains with the Midrash of the coins that every person is a different stamp of the image of G-d, and that the face shows what is inside a person, citing the wisdom of reading faces in the Zohar on Yisro. He concludes that one cannot hold it against another that he thinks differently.

title.en: The housewife and the cat; the Kohen's brachah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan compared himself and his Zionist secretary to a housewife and a cat: both want no mice, but only the cat enjoys finding them. He then brings the Imrei Emes' answer why a Kohen does not bless 'who did not make me a Yisrael': it would be gaining honor through another's shame.

title.en: Seeing the good, and never cursing a Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that the Torah first mentions the pig's kosher sign before its flaw, that Chazal instituted silent prayer so sinners would not be shamed, and brings the story in Chovos HaLevavos of the chassid who saw a carcass's white teeth. He warns never to curse or speak badly of a Jew except for the sake of Heaven, proves from yibum that one may not say 'may his name be erased' even of an apostate, and cites the Satmar Rav who said he never cursed a Jew.

title.en: Children, Purim jokes and the Torah reader

summary.en: The Mashgiach warns against quizzing other people's children to embarrass them and against Purim jokes at another's expense, explains that one corrects a Torah reader only for a mistake that changes the meaning, notes the custom of singing during a chasan's drashah, and closes with the Chofetz Chaim, who had gebrokts served for a guest so as not to offend him.

catalogTitle: תיקון המדות הנוגע למעשה - דוגמאות וסיפורים

oneLiner.en: Through many examples and stories of gedolim, the Mashgiach shows how careful one must be with another person's feelings and dignity, and ties the low state of middos to churban, past and present.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the churban that came through sinas chinam, and with the Maharal's reading that Kamtza, who did nothing, was blamed as the friend of the one who made the machlokes. From the passuk that Hashem judges 'every hidden thing' he moves to hidden wrongs between people: disgusting habits in front of others, staring at a blemish, embarrassing questions, unclear letters, names that shame a child. A nisayon can come at any moment, as in the story of R' Yosef tested by a poor guest. He shows how halachah itself avoids shaming the poor and the unlearned, and tells many stories of the Chasam Sofer, R' Akiva Eiger, R' Yisrael Salanter, R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld and others. He says great rabbanim attributed the churban in Europe to low middos, warns of the danger facing Klal Yisrael today, and calls for teshuvah as Shavuos approaches.

en: Every punishment reveals its sin: the Beis HaMikdash was destroyed through sinas chinam, and even the friend of a baal machlokes shares the blame.
Hashem judges even 'hidden' wrongs that people do not count as sins, such as behaving disgustingly in front of others or causing someone embarrassment.
What distinguishes an eved Hashem is not the big mitzvos everyone keeps but a hundred small things, above all in how he treats people.
Halachah and Jewish custom were built to avoid shaming those who have less, as with the wood for a tamei korban Pesach, the baal korei and the borrowed clothes of Tu B'Av.
Heaven is exacting about the feelings of others: the stories of Levi, R' Mordechai Banet and the soul that came to R' Moshe of Savran show punishment for causing distress or shame.
The Mashgiach reports hearing from great rabbanim that the churban in Europe came because middos had fallen so low, and he warns of the danger facing Klal Yisrael today.
With Shavuos approaching, he calls for teshuvah and for accepting the yoke of Torah, mitzvos and fear of Heaven, turning only to the Ribono shel Olam.

title.en: Sinas chinam and the friend of Bar Kamtza

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every punishment reveals the sin behind it, so the churban shows it came from sinas chinam. He asks why the Gemara blames Kamtza, who did nothing, and brings the Maharal: Kamtza was the friend of the man who made the machlokes.

title.en: Hidden wrongs between people

summary.en: From the passuk that Hashem judges every hidden thing, the Mashgiach lists wrongs people do not see as sins: disgusting habits in front of others, staring at a blemish, asking one's rebbi an unprepared question in public, and writing letters and addresses unclearly.

title.en: Names that shame a child; the Bas Ayin's Hadas

summary.en: The Mashgiach warns against giving a child a name he will be ashamed of among his friends, and tells of the Bas Ayin in Tzfas who insisted a girl be named Hadas rather than Hadassah, which seventeen years later made her shidduch possible.

title.en: Small things make the eved Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of davening a long Shemoneh Esrei where one does not block others, of listening attentively when someone speaks, and says the eved Hashem is recognized in a hundred small things. He brings R' Sholom of Belz on the 'frummer' and says a person can be tested at any moment, even while leading his child to the chuppah.

title.en: R' Yosef and the hungry guest

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of R' Yosef, a tzaddik who took in the guests nobody wanted, who was tested by the Satan disguised as a starving poor man, and passed. He adds the story of Dovid HaMelech and Nasan HaNavi: a person never knows when his test comes.

title.en: Doing a favor completely

summary.en: The Mashgiach says a person with good middos marks his house number clearly and says a phone number slowly. He tells of a young Belzer Rebbe who as a child told the exact time, and of R' Elchonon Wasserman, who asked a driver to take him all the way to the house: a chessed should be done completely.

title.en: Halachah that protects the poor from shame

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Shechinah stands with the poor man, and shows from a tamei korban Pesach burned with Mikdash wood, from the baal korei, from singing at a hakafah of yichus, and from the borrowed clothes of Tu B'Av that Chazal built practices to avoid shaming. He gives the rule of 'what is hateful to you, do not do to your friend'.

title.en: Appeasing, private tzedakah, and Levi

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one who shamed a friend must appease him, even by letter, and that tzedakah to a person of good family should be given privately. He brings the Gemara that Levi was kept outside the heavenly beis medrash for not attending R' Afes's shiurim and causing him distress.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer's delayed teshuvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the story behind a teshuvah of the Chasam Sofer about reburying R' Mordechai Banet in Nikolsburg. The answer was held back six months because R' Mordechai Banet appeared in a dream: he had to remain buried there for six months, for not defending a girl who was shamed by a broken shidduch.

title.en: A sharp bochur and a soul seeking tikkun

summary.en: Through R' Shlomo Bloch the Mashgiach tells of a great rosh yeshiva whose children died, because as a bochur he had shamed a visiting rav in public. Then he tells of a soul that came to R' Moshe of Savran: it had repented for everything except shaming a chassan who erred in Tehillim before his father-in-law.

title.en: R' Akiva Eiger guards others' honor

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells three stories of R' Akiva Eiger: he kept silent at shared sheva brachos so as not to outshine another chassan, spilled his own wine at the Seder when a guest spilled his, and left a kushya of R' Mordechai Banet unanswered in public so as not to embarrass the town's rav. He then warns young people against nicknames.

title.en: R' Yisrael Salanter and the shamed shoemaker

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how R' Yisrael Salanter gave up a rosh yeshiva position rather than overshadow the other rosh yeshiva, and how he said the rabbanim of Vilna would be held accountable when a rich man shamed a shoemaker at his daughter's chuppah. He then says he heard from great rabbanim that the churban in Europe came because middos had sunk so low.

title.en: The Imrei Emes' warning and today's danger

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Imrei Emes' drashah at the Knessia Gedolah on 'Vayischazeik Dovid', understood only after the churban of Hitler, and the Gemara that the world trembled until the Torah was given. He describes the danger to Eretz Yisrael today and tells how his father-in-law's kehillah in Vienna argued over petty matters while Hitler threatened.

title.en: Not relying on America; teshuvah before Shavuos

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Jews cannot rely on America, now that it no longer needs Israel against Russia, and warns that rising racism and antisemitism resemble how things began in Germany. The only answer is teshuvah, tefillah and tzedakah; Sivan is a time of teshuvah, as Klal Yisrael came to Sinai in teshuvah, and one must accept the yoke of Torah.

title.en: R' Yisrael Salanter: the maid and his last night

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how R' Yisrael Salanter agreed to eat at a wealthy host only if the Shabbos meal took an hour and a half, to spare the tired widow who served. Then he tells of his last night, when he spent his final moments calming his roommate's fear of being alone with a dead body.

title.en: A kept secret and a kerosene cholent

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how R' Yitzchak Elchanan refused even a hundred rubles to reveal who a collection was for, and the donor then confided that he too had lost his fortune. Then R' Avigdor Halberstam, brother of the Divrei Chaim, ate a whole pot of cholent cooked with kerosene so the hostess would not be shamed.

title.en: R' Shmuel Salant, the shofar, and the brazen

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how R' Shmuel Salant rebuked students who laughed at an old woman's question, and how he told a baal tokea that he failed because he felt pride at another's failure. He tells of the Chofetz Chaim expelling a bochur who was insolent to his host, explaining from the Mishnah that the brazen never do teshuvah, and of the Satmar Rav expelling a bochur who refused to collect money.

title.en: R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld's sensitivity

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld spared the Lubliner Rav's feelings when visitors came only to him, gave the Mussaf to the late chazzan's son to comfort the widow, and asked to return to the Old City before his passing so the people carrying him would not have far to go.

catalogTitle: תיקון המדות הנוגע למעשה - ספורי צדיקים

oneLiner.en: Through practical examples and many stories of tzaddikim, the Mashgiach teaches that refined middos mean constant chesed in small things and taking great care never to embarrass or pain another Jew.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with everyday chesed: writing clearly, putting a visible address on a house so Hatzalah can find it, giving a phone number slowly, and not pushing into a line, which can cause a chillul Hashem. Doing chesed, he says, draws chesed onto oneself. He then shows how Jewish customs are built on not shaming those who cannot: singing during a chasan's drasha, the baal korei reading for everyone, the mesader kiddushin saying the brachah, and the daughters of Yerushalayim borrowing garments. A long chain of stories follows: R' Nachum of Chernobyl and the spoon, R' Levi Yitzchak's matzah takanah, R' Mordechai Benet's punishment for a shamed kallah, R' Akiva Eiger, R' Yisrael Salanter and the cook, the Chofetz Chaim, R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld, R' Chaim Ozer and the Satmar Rav. In each, a tzaddik goes out of his way to spare another person's feelings.

en: Small courtesies, like a clear address or a phone number said slowly, are real chesed, and through them a person draws Hashem's chesed onto himself.
Many minhagim, such as singing during the chasan's drasha and the baal korei reading for everyone, exist so as not to shame those who cannot.
Heaven is exacting with tzaddikim even over causing shame indirectly, as R' Mordechai Benet's burial away from Nikolsburg showed.
A person must be farginen, glad for another's success, and lacking this is a deep flaw in middos.
The Chofetz Chaim requires one who spoke lashon hara to appease the victim, but R' Yisrael Salanter held that one should not do so if telling him would cause him pain.
A tzaddik who is used to thinking of another's feelings finds, in the moment, a way to spare him shame or trouble, even at a cost to himself.

title.en: Chesed in everyday small things

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists small acts of chesed: writing legibly, a clear house address so Hatzalah can find it, not pushing into a line, which can make a chillul Hashem, and saying a phone number slowly. He concludes that doing chesed draws chesed onto oneself.

title.en: Minhagim built on not shaming others

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that singing during the chasan's drasha, the baal korei reading for everyone, and the mesader kiddushin saying the brachah all exist so as not to shame those who cannot. He brings the daughters of Yerushalayim borrowing garments and the bikkurim baskets, and applies it to not making an extravagant wedding.

title.en: R' Nachum of Chernobyl and R' Levi Yitzchak

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how R' Nachum of Chernobyl said he gave a poor man the silver spoon he took, and then gave him more for the shame he suffered. Then R' Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, asked for stricter matzah takanos, ruled that one may not knead Jewish blood into the matzos by pressuring the poor women who bake them.

title.en: R' Mordechai Benet and the shamed kallah

summary.en: R' Mordechai Benet died away from Nikolsburg, and the Chasam Sofer delayed his ruling on reburial for six months after R' Mordechai appeared in a dream: he had ruled correctly that a shidduch could be broken, yet a kallah was shamed, and his punishment was to lie beside her. The Mashgiach adds the mashal of an ink stain on a sack versus a silk shirt: tzaddikim are judged to a hairsbreadth.

title.en: R' Akiva Eiger's sensitivity

summary.en: At his Seder, R' Akiva Eiger spilled his own wine after a guest spilled his, saying the table was crooked. When he could not answer R' Mordechai Benet's kushya at a drasha, he later gave the answer privately, explaining he would not shame the rav of the city; R' Mordechai Benet then publicly repeated the answer the next day.

title.en: Nicknames, a shamed shoemaker, and farginen

summary.en: The Mashgiach warns against nicknames and tells of a former shoemaker in Vilna shamed on the way to his son's chuppah, after which R' Yisrael Salanter said the earlier rabbanim of Vilna were judged for not teaching mussar. He stresses farginen, citing Aharon's joy at Moshe's mission and the moon's flaw.

title.en: The Chofetz Chaim and appeasing after lashon hara

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the impact of the sefer Chofetz Chaim, the Gerrer Rebbe's letter urging Chassidim to learn it, and how it healed the rift between Chassidim and Misnagdim. He brings the Chofetz Chaim's ruling that one must appease the person spoken against, and R' Yisrael Salanter's disagreement: telling him would only cause him pain.

title.en: R' Yisrael Salanter and the widowed cook

summary.en: R' Yisrael Salanter agreed to eat at a rich man's Shabbos meal only if it lasted two hours. Afterwards he called in the cook, a widow, who told how the long meals exhausted her, showing the host why he had asked to hurry.

title.en: Chesed until the last moment

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a great chassid who held a separate Friday night table for taxi drivers, of a rebbetzin carrying food to poor families, and of a tzaddik who on his last night calmed his roommate's fear of the dead, so that he would not be frightened when he passed away beside him.

title.en: R' Yitzchak Elchanan and the Dukla Rav

summary.en: A rav arriving in Brisk refused to sit until the delegations of tailors and shoemakers were invited. R' Yitzchak Elchanan refused to reveal for whom he was collecting even when a donor offered more, and the donor turned out to be the impoverished man himself. The Dukla Rav ate an entire cholent spoiled with kerosene so the maid would not be shouted at.

title.en: Not mocking, and the brazen bochur

summary.en: R' Yisrael Salanter answered a simple woman's question about a cat seriously and rebuked his laughing students. The Mashgiach tells of two bochurim: one who sinned was kept in the yeshiva, while one who insulted the woman who fed him was sent away, explained by 'az panim l'Gehinom', since a brazen person does not do teshuvah. He adds the Satmar Rav's guidance and his emphasis on tzedakah.

title.en: R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld's consideration

summary.en: R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld let the son of a deceased baal mussaf lead the Yamim Noraim prayers so his widowed mother would be comforted. When old and ill, he asked to return to the cramped Old City so that the people carrying his coffin would not have far to walk.

title.en: The Chofetz Chaim at the window; R' Moshe Kliers' eruv

summary.en: R' Meir Dan Plotzki persuaded the Chofetz Chaim to show himself at a train window so the crowd would have pleasure. R' Moshe Kliers learned a sugya with the Sephardi chacham whose eruv was questioned, and when the chacham realized his error, reassured him that for kavod habriyos and kavod chachamim one could rely on the eruv. The Mashgiach notes that many do not make this calculation.

title.en: R' Chaim Ozer, the seforim seller, and the Satmar Rav

summary.en: R' Chaim Ozer chose the plainer apartment so the maid would not walk far from kitchen to table. A tzaddik bargained over a sefer so the seller would not regret his price, and the Satmar Rav gave a man $9,500 rather than the $10,000 he asked, for the same reason. The Mashgiach closes on doing chesed so the other does not feel it.

catalogTitle: The Hidden נס of the מגילה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows children that the Megillah is full of hidden miracles, cloaked in nature like the month of Adar, and that Purim trains a person to find Hashem behind everything that happens.

abstract.en: Speaking to boys, the Mashgiach says Purim is not a costume holiday but the foundation of emunah. Yet before the Megillah we bless Hashem for making miracles, and walking through the story he finds none: unlike the plagues and the splitting of the Sea, everything could have been read in a newspaper. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar's parable of a dying man for whom an unexpected doctor and an unexpected medicine arrive at the same moment, and adds his own image of a watch that reassembles itself when shaken. Then he explains two kinds of miracles: those that break nature, like the manna, and nature itself, which only habit hides. Nisan is the month of open miracles; Adar, from 'aderes', a cloak, is the month of cloaked ones. The Megillah's perfect timing, and events in our own day, show Hashem's hand. Purim, he concludes, trains a person to find Hashem in his own life.

en: Purim is not a Jewish Halloween but, the Mashgiach says, the foundation of emunah in the Ribono shel Olam.
Read on the surface, the Megillah has no open miracle: every event is natural, unlike the plagues and the splitting of the Sea.
There are two kinds of miracles: those where Hashem changes nature, and those hidden inside nature, which people take for granted only because they are used to them.
Nisan is the month of open miracles, while Adar, related to 'aderes', a cloak, is the month of miracles cloaked in nature.
In golus Hashem hides in nature, but the Megillah shows His hand through perfect timing: each event happened exactly when it was needed.
Purim teaches how to read the Megillah, history and current events, and to find Hashem hiding in one's own life, as in a game of hide-and-seek.

title.en: Searching the Megillah for miracles

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the boys that Purim is not a Jewish Halloween but the foundation of emunah, and notes that before the Megillah we bless Hashem for making miracles. He then walks through the whole story, contrasts it with the plagues and the splitting of the Sea, and finds no miracle at all: everything could have been read in a newspaper.

title.en: The doctor, the medicine and the watch

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar's parable of a man with two hours to live, whose only cure is a medicine six months away that only a distant doctor can give, until both the doctor and the medicine unexpectedly arrive at the door. He asks whether that is not a miracle, and adds a parable of a watch taken apart and put in a can, which reassembles itself when shaken.

title.en: Two kinds of miracles: Nisan and Adar

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains two kinds of miracles: the manna, which breaks nature, and wheat growing from the ground, which is no less a miracle but is taken for granted; he brings the Chasam Sofer's picture of the generation born in the desert who saw bread grow from the ground as a wonder. Nisan is named for the open miracles of the Exodus, while Adar, from 'aderes sei'ar', a cloak, is the month of cloaked miracles.

title.en: Hidden miracles in the Megillah and today

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the open miracles of the Beis HaMikdash with golus, where Hashem is shrouded in nature, and goes back through the Megillah showing how each event came exactly when it was needed. He tells of the Iraqi Scud missiles, where only one man was killed, a man the Steipler had cursed, and brings the Midrash that 'the King' in the Megillah refers to the Ribono shel Olam.

title.en: Purim as hide-and-seek with Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that Purim teaches how to read the Megillah, history and current events, calling it a game of hide-and-seek in which Hashem says 'find Me'. The costumed visitor at the seudah shows that all the world's rulers are only cloaked, and the same Hashem who made the plagues and the manna makes miracles today. He tells the boys to train themselves to look for Hashem in everything that happens and to know He takes care of them.

catalogTitle: ביאור על פי פשט בעשר ספירות

oneLiner.en: In the days of sefirah, when the midos are to be refined, the Mashgiach explains the ten sefiros in simple terms as the ten utterances of creation and the seven midos every person carries.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by noting that the days of sefirah are the time to refine one's midos, and that the Tanya, unlike seforim on the parsha, explains matters step by step. He identifies the ten utterances with which the world was created with the ten sefiros, a key to much in Chassidic seforim. He divides them into the upper three and the seven lower ones, and explains that time itself is a creation, so the Torah's preceding the world by two thousand years means two levels above chesed. He then explains each midah: chesed as giving, gevurah as withdrawal, tiferes as a beautiful blend like a picture of many colors, netzach and hod as winning and yielding, yesod as guarding the bris, and malchus as accepting Heaven's rule. He ties the weeks of sefirah to the midos, explains chochmah and binah, and closes with the Ba'al Shem Tov on misused chesed.

en: The Mashgiach says the days of sefirah are the time to refine the midos, and the Tanya explains them in an orderly way, from the easy matters upward.
The ten utterances of creation are the ten sefiros: three upper ones above the world, and seven lower ones that are the midos a person has.
Chesed is giving out of oneself, gevurah is pulling back into oneself, and tiferes is the blend of the two, as in Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov.
Netzach and hod give a person a firm existence, one by winning and the other by yielding; yesod is guarding the bris, and malchus is accepting the rule of Heaven.
Each week of sefirah refines one midah, and since every midah contains all the others, each day is a different combination.
Above the seven midos are the mochin: chochmah is acquiring knowledge, and binah is building one idea on another to reach a new understanding.

title.en: Sefirah, the Tanya, and the ten utterances

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the days of sefirah are for refining the midos and explains why he learns Tanya: its advice in avodas Hashem, and its orderly explanation of matters rather than drush on the parsha. He then states that the ten utterances of creation are called the ten sefiros, a key to much in Chassidic seforim.

title.en: Three upper sefiros, seven midos, and time

summary.en: The Mashgiach divides the sefiros into the upper three and the seven lower ones that parallel the seven days of creation, and names them all. He asks how the Torah could precede the world by two thousand years when there was no time before creation, and answers that time itself was created, so the 'years' are levels above chesed.

title.en: Chesed, gevurah and tiferes

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains chesed as giving out of oneself, gevurah as its opposite, holding back into oneself, and tiferes as a blend of the two, matching Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov. He illustrates tiferes with the colors of the midos, white and red making pink, and a picture whose beauty comes from the harmony of many colors.

title.en: Netzach, hod and yesod

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains netzach as winning over another, with a mashal of a man with a stick who overcomes a dog, and hod as bowing and yielding; both give a person a lasting existence. He then explains that yesod is connected to the bris kodesh and is called foundation because guarding it is the foundation of Yiddishkeit.

title.en: Malchus, and midos before Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes malchus as awe and accepting the yoke of Heaven, and speaks of serving Hashem with love and with fear, and of tzaddikim who served with netzach or with yesod. He explains that after leaving Mitzrayim one must refine the midos in order to merit receiving the Torah.

title.en: The weeks of sefirah and their midos

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through the weeks of sefirah: the first week repairs chesed, love that has been turned to bad things; the second repairs gevurah, whose holy form is fear of Hashem; and so on to malchus. He explains that each midah contains all the others, chesed shebechesed, gevurah shebechesed and so on, and applies it to the days of the current week.

title.en: The mochin, and chesed misused

summary.en: The Mashgiach links the seven midos to the limbs of the body and to Avraham, Yitzchak, Yaakov, Moshe, Aharon, Yosef and Dovid, then explains the mochin above them: chochmah as learning knowledge, binah as building on it to make a chiddush, and da'as. He closes with the passuk in Kedoshim calling a forbidden relationship 'chesed' and the Ba'al Shem Tov's explanation, concluding that the midos must be refined.

catalogTitle: צירוף החודש - יתהלל המתהלל השכל ויודע - לימוד תורה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the letter combination of the month of Iyar, drawn from the passuk 'yishallel hamishallel haskel veyado'a', marks Iyar as the month of Torah, and calls for strengthening in learning, davening and counting Sefirah, ending with Rosh Chodesh as the day of Dovid HaMelech.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Bnei Yissaschar that each month has its own combination of the letters of Hashem's Name, to be borne in mind at Mussaf of Rosh Chodesh. Nisan's is the straight order; Iyar's, from the initials of 'yishallel hamishallel haskel veyado'a' in Yirmiyahu, reverses the second half and carries some din. Knowing Hashem means seeing Him filling every place, and more inwardly, understanding Torah, which is G-dliness itself. He tells the bochurim that kavanos are not for everyone, then brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the mann began falling in Iyar and Miriam's well came, with the Arizal giving Rav Chaim Vital its water to drink: Iyar is the month of Torah. The days of Sefirah judge a person more than Tishrei and are days of cleansing; the week of Tiferes is Torah. He closes with the two simanim in Shulchan Aruch on the Rosh Chodesh meal and melaveh malkah, both tied to Dovid HaMelech.

en: Each month has its own combination of the letters of Hashem's Name; Iyar's comes from the initials of 'yishallel hamishallel haskel veyado'a' and has the hei before the vav, a touch of din.
Knowing Hashem means recognizing that He fills and surrounds every place, and more inwardly, understanding Torah, which is G-dliness itself.
Iyar is the month of Torah: the mann began to fall in it and Miriam's well came then, and Chazal say the Torah was given only to those who ate the mann.
The days of Sefirah leave a deeper mark on a Jew than Tishrei; they are judgment with chesed and days of cleansing the seven middos.
The Rosh Chodesh meal and melaveh malkah each have a siman in Shulchan Aruch, and both belong to Dovid HaMelech.

title.en: The letter combination of Iyar

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar that each month has its own combination of Hashem's Name, and shows that Iyar's comes from 'yishallel hamishallel haskel veyado'a'. He explains knowing Hashem as seeing Him in all of creation and, more inwardly, as understanding Torah.

title.en: Kavanos, the mann and Miriam's well

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the bochurim that kavanos are not for everyone and that one should daven with the meaning of the words. He then brings the Bnei Yissaschar that Iyar is the month of Torah because the mann fell and Miriam's well came in it, with the Arizal and Rav Chaim Vital at the Kinneret, and ties Iyar to chochmah and the tefillin of Rabbeinu Tam.

title.en: The days of Sefirah and the week of Tiferes

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls for strengthening in Torah as the new zman begins in Iyar, and brings Rav Pinchas of Koretz that the days of Sefirah judge a person more than Tishrei, with din tempered by chesed. He explains the week of Tiferes as Torah and Yaakov Avinu, and urges counting Sefirah with a minyan and with fervor.

title.en: Rosh Chodesh and melaveh malkah, the day of Dovid

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes two simanim in Shulchan Aruch, on the Rosh Chodesh meal and on melaveh malkah, and explains that both belong to Dovid HaMelech: the three Shabbos meals match the three tefillos of the Avos, and melaveh malkah matches tikkun chatzos. Rosh Chodesh, the renewal of the moon, is Dovid's day and a sign of the redemption, and he ends with a l'chaim and a wish for Torah.

catalogTitle: יום שכל יהודי נכנס בפנמיותו - ה'סוד' שיש בו (שייכות לפרשת אמור)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew carries an inner point of holiness, a 'Holy of Holies' in the heart where all Jews are equal, and that Lag BaOmer, the day of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, is the day this secret point is revealed, so that even the lowest Jew can draw strength from it.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Midrash on parshas Emor, 'imros Hashem imros tehoros': learning even about tumah brings purity, and the days of Sefirah are days of purification. He then asks why Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's passing is a day of joy, and why the Beis Aharon says that Rashbi is 'for everyone, even the lowest', when his teaching is the hidden Torah. Through the sefirah of hod, which the Gemara links to the Beis Hamikdash, he shows that Aharon HaKohen is the living Beis Hamikdash, the Holy of Holies of the Jewish people. Every Jew has such an inner point where he cannot be a rasha and where all are equal; this explains the minyan, the mumim of the kohanim, the sin of Rabbi Akiva's students, and why the Kohen Gadol does not mourn. Rashbi, the Holy of Holies after the churban, revealed the inner Torah, so his day has no mourning and every Jew can take chizuk from it.

en: Learning the Torah's portions about tumah does not draw impurity onto a person; Hashem's words are pure and bring purity, especially in the days of Sefirah.
Hod is the power to bow and submit to Hashem, to tzaddikim and to the Torah, and the Gemara calls the Beis Hamikdash 'hod'.
Everything in creation exists in place, time and soul; the Holy of Holies, Yom Kippur and the Kohen Gadol are the innermost point of each, so Aharon is the living Beis Hamikdash.
Every Jew has an inner point that is truly G-dly, that can never be extinguished, and in which the worst Jew is equal to the greatest.
Because every Jew has a unique purpose, every Jew deserves respect; Rabbi Akiva's students failed in this, and Lag BaOmer repairs their sin.
Rashbi is the Holy of Holies and Kohen Gadol of the world, who revealed the hidden Torah after the churban, so his day is joy without mourning.
Faith that one carries this secret point in the heart lets even the lowest Jew draw chizuk from Rashbi on Lag BaOmer and not give up.

title.en: Pure words in the parshiyos of tumah

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Midrash on Emor, 'imros Hashem imros tehoros'. Though speaking of bad things can draw bad onto a person, learning the Torah's portions of tumah in the Sefirah weeks brings purity, refined 'seven times seven'.

title.en: Why Rashbi's passing is a day of joy

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the hilula of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is a joy when other tzaddikim's yahrzeits are not, and finds an earlier answer unsatisfying. He brings the Beis Aharon that whoever believes in Rashbi can draw chizuk from him, 'for all, even the lowest', and asks why, since Rashbi's mark is the hidden Torah meant for the few.

title.en: The seven middos and the week of hod

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that each Sefirah week refines one middah toward Hashem: love, fear and beauty only for Him. Netzach and hod are a person's two legs: netzach stands firm against opposition, while hod bends like grass in the wind; a Jew's beauty is his ability to submit.

title.en: Aharon HaKohen, the living Beis Hamikdash

summary.en: From the Gemara in Berachos that hod is the Beis Hamikdash, the Mashgiach explains why Aharon embodies hod. Using olam, shanah, nefesh, he shows that the Kohen Gadol is the Holy of Holies in the realm of souls, and that Aharon's death in Av, the month of hod, foreshadowed the churban.

title.en: The inner point in every Jew

summary.en: The world is a camouflage over Hashem's presence, and its inner point is G-dliness itself. Likewise every Jew has an inner point that is G-dly, never extinguished and equal in all Jews, like the circle of tzaddikim and the Chasam Sofer's reading of 'like the children of Kush'. It is a private Holy of Holies that a person himself cannot enter.

title.en: The minyan and the Kohen without blemish

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how the minyan for a davar shebikdusha can be learned from the meraglim, reshaim, and answers that ten Jews reveal the inner point where none is a rasha, so ten reshaim make a minyan and nine tzaddikim do not. He adds the Ramban on why the parsha of mumim names the sons of Aharon and not Aharon: in that inner point there is no blemish.

title.en: Every Jew's unique purpose and Rabbi Akiva's students

summary.en: Based on 've'ameich kulam tzaddikim', the Mashgiach explains that every Jew has a unique purpose, as every face differs, in which even the worst Jew is greater than the greatest tzaddik; so one must respect every Jew. Rabbi Akiva's students died for lacking this, and he then taught 'love your fellow as yourself' as the great principle, being himself the inner soul of Klal Yisroel.

title.en: The Beis Hamikdash, place of bowing and equality

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Beis Hamikdash, the place of hod, is always tied to bowing, and that there even a king receives no special honor, for all are equal before Hashem. Since it is the place of the united soul of Klal Yisroel, sinas chinam struck at its very essence.

title.en: Mourning belongs to the outside, not the inner self

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban's parable of the king's children on 'banim atem... lo sisgodedu': a Jew who passes away returns to his Father, so excessive mourning is forbidden. Mourning comes from the body, not the inner soul; Chazal derive it from 'I will turn your festivals into mourning', and Tisha B'Av falls on the weekday of Pesach. Thus the Kohen Gadol, the inner point, barely mourns.

title.en: Rashbi, the Holy of Holies after the churban

summary.en: From 'lo sisgodedu' the Mashgiach shows that all Jewish souls are one, and that the Torah too has an inner part, sod, about G-dliness itself. After the churban Hashem sent Rashbi's soul to take the Beis Hamikdash's place; hidden in the cave he revealed the secrets of the Torah, and as the world's Kohen Gadol, his day of passing has no mourning, only joy.

title.en: The week of hod and the crowds at Meron

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects this to the custom of the Ba'al Shem Tov's disciples to celebrate the yahrzeits of masters of the inner Torah. The week of hod begins with Pesach Sheni, when even the tamei were granted a share, and peaks at Lag BaOmer. That is why all kinds of Jews, even those far from Yiddishkeit, are drawn to Meron: their inner point, where there is no blemish, pulls them to Rashbi.

title.en: Emunah in the hidden point, the meaning of the Beis Aharon

summary.en: Returning to the Beis Aharon, the Mashgiach explains that 'emunah in Rashbi' is not intellectual entry into the pardes, which is forbidden to most, but faith and instinct that one's heart holds a secret, shining point. 'Ohr' equals 'raz': the secret is hidden yet gives light, which is why simple Jews dance with joy over the secrets of the Torah.

title.en: Chizuk for the broken Jew of ikvesa d'meshicha

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks to the Jew broken by the yetzer hara in ikvesa d'meshicha, who feels unworthy of tefillin or a kapitel Tehillim: on Lag BaOmer he must take chizuk and carry it through the year. The day repairs the sin of Rabbi Akiva's students, since even the lowest has a point deserving honor; it is hod shebehod, and it always falls on Purim's weekday.

title.en: Tzedakah of time and a closing wish

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the beis medrash initiative of giving 'tzedakah of time', learning at night with weaker bochurim, and urges joining it, noting that whoever gives his time for another loses nothing. He closes with the wish that everyone feel the secret of the day: that every Jew carries the inner G-dliness of the hidden Torah.

catalogTitle: A Remembrance for the Forgotten Jew (Connection to פרשת פקודי)

oneLiner.en: Through the extra silver of the half-shekel that Moshe Rabbeinu forgot and that became the hooks outside the Mishkan, the Mashgiach shows that Hashem never rejects even the most distant Jew, and that Purim, especially in a year of Adar Sheni, belongs to the forgotten Jews of our generation.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Maggid's test of the Ba'al HaTanya as ba'al koreh: every sedra speaks to its week, and the Adar parshiyos tell of Purim. The silver of the half-shekel of 600,000 Jews made exactly the hundred adanim, which carry Hashem's name; the silver of the extra 3,550 Moshe forgot, until Rabbi Akiva's soul reminded him it became the hooks outside the holiness. Every Jew is a letter of the Torah, and those at the end, like the tribe of Dan cast out of the camp, are the ones Amalek attacks, wrongly thinking Hashem rejected them. The thirteenth month and the Megillah lack Hashem's name; Adar Sheni is the Purim of the forgotten Jew, and Haman repeated Amalek's error. Our generation lives in a double hiding, and Purim grows greater for it. The Mashgiach ends by rebuking indifference to Jews in trouble and urging tefillah in the double Adar.

en: The half-shekel of exactly 600,000 Jews made the hundred adanim, whose name contains Hashem's name, while the silver of the extra 3,550 became the hooks that stood outside the holiness of the Mishkan.
Every Jew is a letter of the Sefer Torah, and none is rejected by Hashem: Amalek attacked the outcasts of the tribe of Dan thinking Hashem had cast them off, and Purim refutes him.
The thirteenth month has no combination of Hashem's four-letter name and the Megillah has no mention of His name; Adar Sheni is therefore the Purim of the Jews in whom Hashem is not seen.
Our generation lives in a double hiding: not only is Hashem hidden, but most Jews do not even know that He is hiding, and the test of the time is to believe that He is there and runs everything.
Purim grows greater with each generation, because the further the Jews fall, the more Purim, the festival of the rejected, belongs to them.

The Mashgiach says that the blame for the lack of salvation lies not with Jews who know nothing but with those raised in Torah, who must not stay indifferent to their brothers' troubles and should use the double Adar for tefillah.

title.en: The Maggid tests the Ba'al HaTanya

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Maggid of Mezritch chose the young Ba'al HaTanya as ba'al koreh after he knew how each sedra, each aliyah and each person called up relates to the week. From this he turns to the Adar parshiyos, which tell of Purim and of the decree against the Jews.

title.en: The adanim and the forgotten silver

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the hundred silver adanim made from the half-shekel of 600,000 Jews. Since the census counted 603,550, there was extra silver; at the accounting Moshe Rabbeinu forgot what he did with it, until, the Midrash says, Rabbi Akiva's soul reminded him that he made the hooks for the pillars of the courtyard.

title.en: Every Jew a letter of the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Moshe forgot and why Rabbi Akiva had to remind him. He describes the camp of four groupings around the Mishkan, and explains that the 600,000 root souls match 600,000 letters of the Torah, so each Jew is a letter whose absence would spoil the Sefer Torah; the five Chumashim mirror the camp.

title.en: Dan outside the camp and Amalek

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that part of the tribe of Dan, always a source of trouble and placed last in the camp, was cast out from under the clouds of glory, and Amalek attacked them thinking Hashem had rejected them. He says Hashem rejects no Jew, not even the worst, and that Purim is the refutation of Amalek's claim to the Jew on the fringe.

title.en: Adar Sheni and the hooks outside

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the thirteenth month has none of the twelve combinations of Hashem's name, like the Megillah, and Adar Sheni is the Purim of Jews in whom Hashem is not seen. The adanim carry Hashem's name, while the forgotten Jews' silver became hooks outside the holiness; yet a vav joins, so even they stay connected to the camp.

title.en: The last eight pesukim and forgetting

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara on who wrote the last eight pesukim of the Torah, Yehoshua or Moshe with tears, and calls them the forgotten pesukim, since Moshe's death and the broken luchos brought forgetting. The souls at the end of the Torah went through forgetting, so Moshe forgot them, and Rabbi Akiva, from a root without forgetting, reminded him.

title.en: Yehoshua against Amalek

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Amalek attacks the souls at the end of the Torah, so Yehoshua, not Moshe, fights Amalek and writes the last pesukim. He brings that only Rachel's children can stand against Esav, as Yosef and Binyamin were not part of the brothers' sale, and that Moshiach ben Yosef will fight Amalek last.

title.en: Haman's shekalim and his mistake

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that in a leap year the Megillah is read in the second Adar, to join redemption to redemption. He then discusses Haman's ten thousand talents against the half-shekel, and shows that Haman paid only for the 600,000, not the 3,550 extra Jews, repeating Amalek's mistake that some Jews are rejected.

title.en: Our generation and the double hiding

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies this to the last generation before Moshiach, the rejected thirteenth month of history, when masses of Jews do not know what Shema Yisrael means; Purim grows greater for them. Through the Gemara on Esther and a parable of a father hidden from his son, he explains the double hiding of today and the test to believe that Hashem is there.

title.en: A call to wake up and daven

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the months when tefillos are accepted, of the promises about this year, and of the yahrzeit of the Rebbe Reb Elimelech, telling how the Belzer Rav waited at the window for Moshiach the year before the war. He says the blame lies with Jews raised in Torah, rebukes indifference to Jews in trouble, and urges using the double Adar for tefillah.

catalogTitle: היום נתגלה נקודה פנימיות של כל ישראל שנקרא קודש קדשים

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai stands above the churban like the hidden Kodesh HaKodashim, and that on Lag Ba'omer the hidden point of love in every Jew, even the most distant, is revealed.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Satmar Rav, who explained the singing in Meron during the Nine Days with the words "oz vechedvah bimkomo", and with the Likutei Torah that the churban had no hold on Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai. He tells of a student of the Arizal punished for saying Nachem on Rashbi's day. In the Kodesh HaKodashim there was no churban: Shlomo HaMelech hid the Aron in tunnels beneath it, and so every Jew's heart holds a hidden point, the ahavah mesuteres, that churban cannot reach. Moshe forgot the vavim made from the half-shekels of the Jews outside the camp, and Rabbi Akiva's soul reminded him; Rashbi, Rabbi Akiva's continuation, declares that Torah and the forgotten Jews are never forgotten. After singing, the Mashgiach explains that on Lag Ba'omer, completing hod shebehod, Klal Yisrael seizes Yishmael's bow, and connects the 70 tikkunim of Rashbi to "vayehi roveh kashes". He closes with a tefillah for kiddush Hashem.

en: The churban had no hold on Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, just as there was no churban in the Kodesh HaKodashim.
Shlomo HaMelech hid the Aron in tunnels under the Beis HaMikdash, and in the same way every Jew's heart holds a hidden point, the concealed love of Hashem, that churban cannot reach.
The Jews who fell outside the camp are the forgotten souls; Rabbi Akiva's soul reminded Moshe of them, and Rashbi carries on that role.
Lag Ba'omer is a secret that Jews feel without understanding: the revealing of the hidden love, which strengthens every Jew, even the posh'im.
Rashbi declares that the Torah will never be forgotten; the Torah is scattered like the Jews in galus, but neither the Torah nor any Jew is forgotten.
On Lag Ba'omer Klal Yisrael seizes Yishmael's weapon, the bow, just as David HaMelech killed Goliath with his own sword.

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Satmar Rav justified singing in Meron during the Nine Days with "oz vechedvah bimkomo", brings the Likutei Torah that the churban did not touch Rashbi, and tells of the Arizal's student who was punished for saying Nachem on Rashbi's day.

title.en: The hidden Aron and the hidden love

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that there was no churban in the Kodesh HaKodashim, since Shlomo HaMelech hid the Aron in tunnels beneath it. He ties Shlomo to Shir HaShirim, the holy of holies, and says every Jew's heart has a hidden point, the ahavah mesuteres, which is the hidden Aron.

title.en: The forgotten vavim and the forgotten souls

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Moshe forgot the vavim, the only part of the Mishkan outside the camp, made from the extra half-shekels of the Jews who fell outside the camp, and that Rabbi Akiva's soul reminded him. He links them to the last eight pesukim of the Torah and the forgotten halachos, and brings Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen on why the hillula is Rashbi's and not Rabbi Akiva's.

title.en: Lag Ba'omer, a secret every Jew feels

summary.en: Bringing the Ba'al HaTanya's siddur that tikkun chatzos mourns Yerushalayim, meaning yiras shamayim, the Mashgiach says there is a hidden point in Yerushalayim and in the Jewish heart that the churban does not touch. Rashbi's day gives chizuk to the distant ones: their hidden love is untouched, and Jews feel the joy of Lag Ba'omer without understanding it. The talk ends with the crowd breaking into song.

title.en: The Torah and the Jews in exile

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara of Kerem B'Yavneh, where Rashbi rejects the fear that the Torah will be forgotten, and explains that the Torah, like the Jews, is scattered in galus, its halachos not in their place. He connects Lag Ba'omer, Purim and the nidachim outside the camp, where forgetting took hold.

title.en: No forgetting on Lag Ba'omer

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how Moshe, who received the Torah like a kallah and never forgot, could forget the vavim, and answers that the Jews are Hashem's kallah, who is never forgotten. Rashbi, the continuation of Rabbi Akiva, reveals on Lag Ba'omer that there is no forgetting, and the Mashgiach ends with the pull of all Jews to Meron.

title.en: Interlude

summary.en: An interlude.

title.en: Seizing Yishmael's bow

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the greatest victory is seizing the enemy's weapon, as David took Goliath's sword. Yishmael's power is the bow, the middah of yesod through milah; sefiras ha'omer repairs yesod, and on Lag Ba'omer, after hod shebehod, Klal Yisrael seizes the bow. He connects "vayehi roveh kashes" to the 70 tikkunim of Rashbi, who repairs all seventy faces of Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Tefillah for the breaking of the bow

summary.en: The Mashgiach closes with a tefillah that Hashem's kingship be revealed, that the kelipah of Yishmael be broken, and that there be a great kiddush Hashem in the world.

catalogTitle: רצה ר' שמעון שישמחו בהילולא שלו

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai wanted his hillula to be a day of joy: Lag Ba'omer reveals the inner core of every Jew, like Yom Kippur and Purim, and is a day of seeking Zion, and he calls on his listeners to thank Hashem for the open miracles He does for the Jews.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Eliyahu's words to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai that through the Zohar the Jews will leave exile, and explains that this includes the chassidic sefarim built on it, since the Ba'al Shem Tov carried Rabbi Shimon's soul. The joy of his hillula is above nature, a joy of the days of Moshiach. Lag Ba'omer is like Yom Kippur and like Purim: all three reveal the inner point of a Jew, the 'rotzeh ani' the Rambam finds in every Jew, and Rabbi Shimon himself taught that the sin in Haman's time was only outward. Counting the omer today is a remembrance of the Beis Hamikdash, a way of seeking Zion, and Lag Ba'omer is a special day of it. Finally the Mashgiach describes the crowds at Meron and the constant miracles in Eretz Yisrael, and says one must thank Hashem.

en: Eliyahu told Rabbi Shimon that through the Zohar the Jews will leave exile, and the Mashgiach explains this includes all the holy sefarim built on it, especially those of the Ba'al Shem Tov's disciples.
The joy of Rabbi Shimon's hillula is above nature, a joy of the days of Moshiach that Jews feel and that cannot be held back.
Lag Ba'omer is both like Yom Kippur and like Purim, and all three reveal the inner core of a Jew.
Counting the omer today is a remembrance of the Beis Hamikdash and a way of seeking Zion, and Lag Ba'omer, which comes from the Holy of Holies, is a special day of seeking Zion.
Hashem does constant open miracles for the Jews in Eretz Yisrael, but people have grown used to them, and the Mashgiach says one must thank Hashem for them, especially in these weeks.

summary.en: After brief opening words that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai wanted his hillula to be joyous, the Mashgiach brings Eliyahu's words that through the Zohar the Jews will leave exile, and explains that the chassidic sefarim built on it are included, since the Ba'al Shem Tov carried Rabbi Shimon's soul. He brings the Ramchal on Moshe's 'shevi', and says the first chassidic sefer was called the Torah of Moshiach, whose Torah is joy.

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Rabbi Shimon wanted joy at his hillula and that this joy is above nature, as the Bnei Yissaschar brings. He tells of the Belzer Rav who called Lag Ba'omer a great day like Yom Kippur, adds that it is also like Purim by the Shulchan Aruch's calendar sign, and explains that Purim reveals the inner core of a Jew.

title.en: 'Rotzeh ani': the inner point of a Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yom Kippur reveals the 'rotzeh ani', the true will of every Jew, from the Rambam, and that it equals Yom Kippur in gematria and corresponds to the fortieth level, the Holy of Holies. He brings Rabbi Shimon's answer in the Gemara that the sin in Haman's time was only outward, and concludes that Lag Ba'omer holds Purim and Yom Kippur together.

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that counting the omer today is a remembrance of the Beis Hamikdash, which the Gemara derives from 'Zion, no one seeks her', and that every such remembrance is a way of seeking Zion that arouses the same above. Lag Ba'omer, which comes from the Holy of Holies, is a special day of seeking Zion.

title.en: Meron this year and the miracles since the Six Day War

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells that the government in Eretz Yisrael tried to keep Jews from Meron for fear of terrorists, yet more Jews came than ever. He recalls the open miracles of the Six Day War, which even the secular papers printed daily, and a reader who asked them to stop because it spoiled her Shabbos trips to the beach.

title.en: Accustomed to miracles

summary.en: Comparing the Jews to Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, who was accustomed to miracles, the Mashgiach asks who holds back the hundreds of millions of Arabs around Eretz Yisrael. He describes a Jerusalem neighborhood bounded only by a road where nothing ever happened, and the enemies who swore revenge yet could do little, while the Americans lose soldiers every week.

title.en: Thanking Hashem in the weeks of hod

summary.en: The Mashgiach laments that people take the miracles lightly and says one must thank Hashem, especially in these weeks, a time of hoda'ah, and not remain ungrateful but take on more Torah, avodas Hashem and good deeds. The shiur closes with a brief exchange about a niggun.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the Beis Aharon's words that just as Hashem is good to all, so Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is for all, even the lowest: Lag Baomer, hod sheb'hod, is the day of the hidden 'sod' in which every Jew carries a secret worth that only the masters of sod perceive.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Beis Aharon: whoever has emunah in Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai has chizuk from him, for he is for all, even the lowest. He sets alongside it the Maggid of Koznitz, who applied 'when will I come and see the face of G-d' to the longing for Lag Baomer. Following the Siddur Baal HaTanya, the week of hod is a second, finishing tikkun of the middos, and since the end is bound to the beginning, the lowest point reveals the highest. Like the Torah, the world has pshat and sod in place, time and soul: the Kodesh haKodashim, the fiftieth day, and Aharon, the soul of sod, for whom there is no aveilus. Rashbi, who revealed the secrets, is the aspect of the Kohen Gadol, so in Meron there is no mourning. In pshat one Jew is greater than another; in sod each is an indispensable letter of the Torah. Rashbi's day therefore gives chizuk even to the lowest.

en: The Beis Aharon teaches that whoever has emunah in Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai draws chizuk from him, for like Hashem he is good to all, even the lowest.
The week of hod in sefirah is a second, overall tikkun of the middos, and at its lowest point, hod sheb'hod, the highest light is revealed, because every end is bound to its beginning.
The world, like the Torah, has levels from pshat to sod in place, time and soul: the Kodesh haKodashim, the fiftieth day, and the soul of Aharon the Kohen Gadol.
In the realm of sod there is no aveilus, since in truth everything from Hashem is chesed; therefore the Kohen Gadol was not bound by mourning, and at Rashbi's place in Meron one does not mourn.
Every Jew is a letter of the Sefer Torah with a virtue no other Jew has, so in sod all Jews are equal and each must be honored, a lesson the students of Rabbi Akiva lacked.
Lag Baomer, like Purim, is a day for the lowly: every Jew carries a secret that only masters of sod like Rashbi understand, and this gives even the lowest chizuk that he is needed.

title.en: The Beis Aharon and longing for Lag Baomer

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Beis Aharon: whoever has emunah in Rashbi has chizuk from him, for he is for all, even the lowest. He brings the Maggid's reading of 'when will I come and see the face of G-d' as the longing for Lag Baomer, and the Siddur Baal HaTanya's account of the sefirah weeks, where the week of hod begins a second tikkun of the middos.

title.en: The end bound to the beginning

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every end is bound to its beginning: the Torah's last parsha, tied to the lowest souls, is joined to Bereishis, the aspect of Moshe and Moshiach. So at hod sheb'hod, the lowest point of the tikkun, the highest light of Moshe, Moshiach and Rashbi is revealed, with joy and the sweetening of judgments.

title.en: Pardes in the world: place and time

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Torah has pshat, remez, drush and sod, and since the world was created from the Torah in place, time and soul, the world too has these levels. In place, Eretz Yisrael is drush and the Kodesh haKodashim is sod, beyond nature; in time, the fiftieth day after seven times seven is above time, which is why Moshe could add a day before Matan Torah.

title.en: Aharon, the soul of sod

summary.en: In the soul, the Mashgiach explains, Aharon is the sod: he alone enters the Kodesh haKodashim, where even angels may not go. Aharon is hod, and the Gemara calls the Beis Hamikdash hod, so he is hod sheb'hod. Therefore the Kohen Gadol does not leave the Mikdash and may serve as an onen: in the world of sod there is no aveilus, for there everything is chesed.

title.en: Rashbi as the Kohen Gadol: no mourning in Meron

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Rashbi, who revealed the secrets of the Torah on Lag Baomer, is the aspect of the Kohen Gadol, as sung in 'Bar Yochai'. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the joy of Lag Baomer is above the natural order, and tells of the Arizal stopping a tzaddik from saying Nachem in Meron and of the Satmar Rav having 'Bar Yochai' sung there in the Nine Days. Lag Baomer reveals geulah, and Shavuos brings one to the yovel and the Beis Hamikdash.

title.en: Interlude

summary.en: An interlude.

title.en: The Maggid's words explained

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Maggid: through sefirah Jews long for hod sheb'hod, the Beis Hamikdash, and 'pnei Elokim' means the innermost part of the name Elokim, which is all mercy. Then the aspect of Moshiach, Rashbi's aspect, is revealed and mourning ceases. He adds that every Jew is a letter of the Sefer Torah, so that a single missing letter would make it invalid.

title.en: Honoring every Jew: pshat and sod

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the students of Rabbi Akiva did not honor one another, which became grave in the days of sefirah. In pshat one Jew is greater than another, like the large beis of Bereishis; in sod all are equal, like the circle dance of the tzaddikim around Hashem, and each has a mission only he can fulfil. Rashbi, a student of Rabbi Akiva, revealed the sod, and with it the duty to honor every Jew.

title.en: Rashbi is for all, even the lowest

summary.en: Returning to the Beis Aharon, the Mashgiach explains that even one who knows nothing of Rashbi's Torah but has emunah in him draws chizuk: every Jew carries a secret, and Rashbi understands every Jew. Like Purim, a day for the lowly, Lag Baomer falls on Purim's weekday, and 'gal' hints to it. He closes on the week of hod as a time when every Jew may enter the gates of tzedek, and returns to the Maggid's longing.

catalogTitle: The Eternal נסים of מגילת אסתר

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the miracles of the Megillah are hidden inside nature, just as Hashem's name is hidden in it, and that reading the Megillah trains a Jew to find Hashem behind world events and his own daily life.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the joy of Adar and asks how we can make the bracha 'she'asa nisim' over a Megillah that reads like an ordinary court story, with no split sea and no mention of Hashem's name. He answers that Nisan, the first month, is the month of revealed miracles, while Adar, the last, means a cloak: its miracles are covered by nature. Nature itself is a miracle, as bread from the ground would be to someone raised on the mann. Through a parable of a dying patient saved by a medicine and a doctor arriving just in time, he shows that the Megillah's nes is a jigsaw puzzle of natural events, and that current events, from the Gulf War onward, are a Megillah being written now. 'HaMelech' means Hashem, rulers are marionettes, and His name hides in the words. Reading the Megillah teaches a Jew to read the world and his own life.

en: The Megillah tells a seemingly natural story with no open miracle and no mention of Hashem's name, yet we make the bracha 'she'asa nisim' over it.
Nisan is the month of revealed miracles; Adar, the month furthest from it, means a cloak, and its miracles are hidden in nature.
Nature itself is a miracle made by the same Hashem who makes open miracles; we fail to see it only because we are used to it.
The nes of the Megillah is a jigsaw puzzle of many small natural events, each one needed, put together by Hashem.
In the Megillah 'HaMelech' alludes to Hashem, and in the same way world leaders are marionettes moved by strings from above.
Hashem's name is in the Megillah, hidden in the first and last letters of words, and one has to look for it.
The Megillah is a drill in reading the world: one who learns to read it can find Hashem in current events and in his own life.

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the joy of Adar and the great kedusha of Megillas Esther, written with ruach hakodesh. He points out that Hashem's name never appears in it and that it reads like a plain court story, and asks how we can then make the bracha 'she'asa nisim'.

title.en: Nisan and Adar: revealed and cloaked miracles

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Nisan, the first month and the month of revealed miracles, with Adar, the last month, whose name means a cloak, as in 'aderes se'ar'. He explains that nature is itself a miracle, using the example of a child raised on the mann who first sees bread grow from the ground.

title.en: Parable of the patient and the medicine

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a parable of a dying patient whose only cure is a medicine from China and a doctor from America, both months away, who both arrive just in time. Nothing supernatural happened, yet anyone sees there was a plan, and this, he says, is the kind of nes in the Megillah.

title.en: The jigsaw puzzle of the Megillah and of today

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows how every detail of the Megillah, from Vashti's removal to Mordechai understanding Bigsan and Teresh and the king's sleepless night, is a screw in one machine. He applies this to current events such as the Gulf War and the fall of Russia, and explains that court gossip a yeshiva boy rightly ignores was, in Achashverosh's time, the unfolding of a nes.

title.en: Why Hashem's name is missing; 'HaMelech'

summary.en: The Mashgiach gives a simple reason why Hashem's name is absent from the Megillah and brings the Midrash that 'HaMelech' alludes to Hashem, comparing it to a believer reading about the president in the newspaper. He brings the passuk that the hearts of kings are in Hashem's hand and Rashi that Amalek conceals Hashem's name and throne.

title.en: Rulers as marionettes

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes a marionette show whose thin strings the audience cannot see. Achashverosh's sudden change from Haman's side to Esther's shows that he was a marionette, and the Mashgiach applies the same to the leaders of his day, who turn this way and that as Hashem pulls the strings.

title.en: Hashem's hidden name in the Megillah and in history

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why some ba'alei kriah read 'Yavo hamelech v'Haman hayom' in one breath: the Arizal explains that its first letters spell Hashem's name, which appears at turning points of the story, sometimes backwards in final letters. Likewise Hashem's hand is hidden in history, where the empires that oppressed the Jews are gone and the Jews live on.

title.en: Learning to read the Megillah and the world

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the bracha 'al mikra Megillah' as learning to read, like a doctor reading an x-ray, and calls the Megillah a drill in finding Hashem in newspapers and history books. With the masked collector at the Purim seudah and a late lunch at home, he concludes that the world is masked, Hashem directs every detail, and one who learns this fears no one.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, on Lag Ba'Omer, sweetens the harsh judgment of hod, turning the 'blood' of din into the 'milk' of chesed that is completed on Shavuos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the great crowds of Jews drawn to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and the miracles and protection seen in his merit. He then explains that the work of the days of sefirah is to sweeten the gevuros, the harsh judgments, through teshuvah, which rises to binah. The hardest of them is hod, the fifth middah, furthest from binah: the Beis Hamikdash, called hod, was destroyed in the fifth millennium, and hod reversed spells the impurity of blood. Lag Ba'Omer, hod shebehod, begins the third part of the count, the dawn watch, when the blood of din starts turning into the milk of chesed, completed on Shavuos; hence dairy on Shavuos. He shows the same pattern in Av, the fifth month, with the passing of Aharon and of the Arizal, and links Rabbi Shimon to the passuk 'al tishkechi kol gemulav'. He closes with the greatness of the day and a story joining nigleh with nistar.

en: The purpose of counting sefirah is to sweeten the gevuros, the attributes of judgment, and teshuvah does this because it reaches binah, above the seven middos.
Hod, the fifth middah, is the harshest judgment because it is the furthest from binah.
The Beis Hamikdash is called hod and was destroyed in the fifth millennium, the time of hod, when hod was overturned.
From Lag Ba'Omer the blood of judgment begins turning into the milk of chesed, and on Shavuos the process is complete, which is why dairy is eaten on Shavuos.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who revealed the inner Torah on the day of his passing, holds the sweetening hidden inside hod.

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that sefirah serves to sweeten the gevuros through teshuvah, which reaches binah, and that hod, furthest from binah, is the hardest judgment. He ties hod to the Beis Hamikdash and its destruction, shows that hod reversed spells the impurity of blood, and explains that Lag Ba'Omer, hod shebehod, begins the dawn watch of the count, citing the Shem MiShmuel.

title.en: Blood becomes milk: from Lag Ba'Omer to Shavuos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that blood turns into milk and explains that the red of din becomes the white of chesed starting on Lag Ba'Omer and ending on Shavuos, the fiftieth day of binah. He brings the poskim's hint for eating dairy on Shavuos from the passuk of the minchah chadashah, and explains the counting from the omer offering as sweetening the dinim.

title.en: Av, the Arizal and Rabbi Shimon

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that Av, the fifth month, is also hod: the Beis Hamikdash was destroyed then, Aharon died on Rosh Chodesh Av, and the Arizal, a gilgul of Rabbi Shimon, passed away on the fifth of Av. He contrasts the Arizal's teachings, which stayed hidden, with Rabbi Shimon's, which also entered the Mishnah and braisos.

title.en: The soul of 'al tishkechi' and the greatness of the day

summary.en: The Mashgiach links the mazal of Av to the overturned hod and Rabbi Shimon to 'al tishkechi kol gemulav', through the Gemara about milk placed at the seat of binah. He then calls the day awesome, says one cannot let it slip away, calls it a day of milk and whiteness, and closes with Rabbi Shimon as one soul spread over all Jews.

He ends noting it is also the Rema's yahrzeit, nigleh joined with nistar.

oneLiner.en: On Lag BaOmer, the Rema's yahrzeit, the Mashgiach suggests that the Rema is the revealed side of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: Rabbi Shimon used the dove and revealed the hidden good in every Jew and even in the tochacha, while the Rema used the raven to uncover what is not in order.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a feeling that the Rema, whose yahrzeit is Lag BaOmer and who is the Rebbe of Ashkenazi Jewry, is the revealed part of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai. He tells how the Maggid of Mezritch smelled chametz at his seder because the Baal HaTanya had kashered a glass cup against the Rema's view, and the Rema came to complain. He then tells how the Rema, as a new rav, exposed a seller of non-kosher fat by seeing ravens over his wagon. Rabbi Shimon, by contrast, answered his students by a dove that everything in the tochacha is blessing. The Mashgiach explains that every Jew is a letter of the Torah holding a secret, that the tochacha hides the secret of the geulah, and that on Lag BaOmer every Jew can find himself in Rabbi Shimon. He closes with Rabbi Shimon's promise that the Torah will not be forgotten.

en: The Mashgiach suggests, as a feeling of his own, that the Rema is the revealed (nigleh) part of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, and that both share Lag BaOmer.
Rabbi Shimon worked with the dove, which brings good tidings, while the Rema worked with the raven, which reveals what is wrong.
Every Jew corresponds to a letter of the Sefer Torah and adds something no other Jew can add, so even the simplest Jew holds a hidden secret.
The tochacha hides the secret of the geulah, and its letters too are Jewish souls.
On Lag BaOmer, even at its lowest level, every Jew can find himself in Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains, through the parsha of the kings of Edom, that the vessels broke because the receivers said "I will rule" instead of submitting to the giver, and that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the secret of the Yovel, repairs this breakage and brings it down to the lowest souls of the last generations.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the joy of Lag BaOmer, which grows from generation to generation because the higher a light is, the lower it reaches. He turns to the parsha of the kings who ruled in Edom, which, as the sefer he reads explains, holds the whole plan of how Hashem runs the world, where in the end kedushah alone will rule. Following the Arizal, he explains that all of creation is giver and receiver; the vessels broke because the receivers said "I will rule", and the sparks fell into the sitra achra. Raising those sparks back to their root is Yovel. Rabbi Shimon, the secret of fifty, descends to the lowest level to repair our souls, and Lag BaOmer is the repair of the breakage. The Mashgiach closes with the love among Rabbi Shimon's companions, the circle of dancers, and Rabbi Shimon's view that all Jews are princes.

en: The joy of Lag BaOmer grows from generation to generation, because the higher a light is, the lower it descends.
The parsha of the kings of Edom contains the whole plan of Hashem's running of the world, whose end is that kedushah alone will rule.
All of creation works as giver and receiver; the vessels broke because the receivers did not submit to the giver but said "I will rule".
A Jew's task is to raise the sparks trapped in the sitra achra, for example by eating with kedushah, and bringing them back to their root is called Yovel.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the secret of fifty, descends to the lowest level to repair the souls of the last generations; Lag BaOmer is the repair of the breakage of "I will rule".
According to Rabbi Shimon all Jews are princes and all are equal, and in the days of Moshiach the halacha will follow him.
